messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero inflated Poisson model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Zero inflated Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
Two years ago, you helped me on this zero inflated Poisson model.  It worked out very well and I completed that project in 2013.

Today, I picked up the code again and wanted to use it for a different problem.  I now use RStan 2.2.0, R 3.1.0, and Xcode 5.1.1 on Mac OSx 10.9.3 (Maverick).  I reran the code using the same data used 2 years ago, but the model crashed.  I have attached the R script file, data, model file, and initial values.  Thank you very much.

fit25 <- stan(model_code=model.file, data=input.data,
+                        init=input.inits,
+                        pars=input.para, chains=n.chains, iter=n.iters)

TRANSLATING MODEL 'model.file' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'input.to.bugs$model' NOW.

 *** caught segfault ***
address 0x20, cause 'memory not mapped'

Traceback:
 1: .Call(Module__functions_names, xp)
 2: Module(module, mustStart = TRUE)
 3: .getModulePointer(x)
 4: <S4 object of class "Module">$stan_fit4model3b9168916c19_input_to_bugs_model
 5: <S4 object of class "Module">$stan_fit4model3b9168916c19_input_to_bugs_model
 6: eval(expr, envir, enclos)
 7: eval(call("$", mod, paste("stan_fit4", model_cppname, sep = "")))
 8: .local(object, ...)
 9: sampling(sm, data, pars, chains, iter, warmup, thin, seed, init,     check_data = TRUE, sample_file = sample_file, diagnostic_file = diagnostic_file,     verbose = verbose, algorithm = match.arg(algorithm), control = control,     ...)
10: sampling(sm, data, pars, chains, iter, warmup, thin, seed, init,     check_data = TRUE, sample_file = sample_file, diagnostic_file = diagnostic_file,     verbose = verbose, algorithm = match.arg(algorithm), control = control,     ...)
11: stan(model_code = input.to.bugs$model, data = input.to.bugs$data,     init = input.to.bugs$inits, pars = input.to.bugs$para, chains = n.chains,     iter = n.iters)

Possible actions:
1: abort (with core dump, if enabled)
2: normal R exit
3: exit R without saving workspace
4: exit R saving workspace
Selection: 3

On Wednesday, September 26, 2012 2:37:22 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This isn't a 1.0.1 vs. 1.0.2 issue if you have the
> transforms matching your truncations.  (I should've
> also pointed out that if the truncation points are
> constant, you don't even need the truncations -- the
> probabilty is still right up to a proportion without it.)
>
> Are you letting Stan do the initializations or
> doing them yourself?  If you are, the inits need to
> be in the support or you'll get the error you report
> because no step size will get the particle moving.
>
> You can try running with the test_grad option to
> see if the initialization is OK -- it'll print out
> the unconstrained (transformed) initial values along with
> the gradients  computed by auto-dif and by finite diffs.
> (The unconstrained params come in the same order as
> the parameter declarations.)
>
> The partials in the gradient should all be finite, or
> there's a problem with the model specification at the
> initialization point.
>
> If you run this and still have problems that aren't
> due to inits, could you send us a copy of the current model
> and data, either to the list or to st...@mc-stan.org?
>
> - Bob
>
> On 9/26/12 2:05 PM, Song S. Qian wrote:
> > Thank you very much for looking over my code. I made the changes you suggested that got the following error message:
> >
> > Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) :
> >    No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?
> >
> > I will wait for 1.0.2.
> >
> > Song
> >
> > On Wed, Sep 26, 2012 at 1:34 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
> >
> >     On 9/26/12 11:44 AM, Song wrote:
> >      > I have a zero-inflated Poisson model problem that I implemented in JAGS.
> >      > ...
> >
> >      > I tried to use
> >      > Stan this week and it worked for the single species model, but with very different results.
> >
> >     Thanks for trying it out.
> >
> >     There are two issues.  A bug on our end and an
> >     error in coding your model.  We're fixing the bug
> >     for 1.0.2, but luckily in this case, recoding the model
> >     with constraints will fix the problem in 1.0.1.
> >
> >     The model coding problem is that need to declare the parameters to
> >     have constraints that match their truncations:
> >
> >      > ...
> >
> >      >                    parameters{
> >      >                      real alpha[2];
> >      >                      real beta[3];
> >      >                    }
> >      >                    model{
> >     ...
> >
> >      >                      alpha[1] ~ normal(10,100);
> >      >                      alpha[2] ~ normal(10,100)T[0,];
> >      >
> >      >                      beta[1] ~ normal(0, 100);
> >      >                      beta[2] ~ normal(0, 100)T[0,];
> >      >                      beta[3] ~ normal(0, 100)T[-1,];
> >
> >     This means you need to define alpha[2], beta[2], and beta[3]
> >     with constraints.  This isn't directly possible in a Stan
> >     array, which requires the same constraint on every entry.
> >
> >     So in this case, I'd just recode as
> >
> >     parameters
> >        real alpha1;
> >        real<lower=0> alpha2;
> >        real beta1;
> >        real<lower=0> beta2;
> >        real<lower=-1> beta3;
> >
> >
> >      >
> >      >                      for(i in 1:NOBS) {
> >      >                        lambda[i] <- exp(beta[1]-beta[2]*x[i]+beta[__3]*log(x[i]));
> >      >                        pi[i] <- inv_logit(alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x[i]);
> >
> >     It's a bit more efficient to define lambda and pi
> >     to be scalars and reuse them (they don't need
> >     to be arrays).
> >
> >
> >      >                        lp__ <- lp__ + if_else(iszero[i], log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i])),
> >      >                                               log1m(pi[i])+poisson_log(Y[i], lambda[i]));
> >
> >     If lambda[i] gets too small (< -800 or so), the
> >     exp(-lambda[i]) will overflow.  In general, log_sum_exp
> >     can be used to avoid the overflow:
> >
> >
> >        log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i]))
> >
> >        ==>
> >
> >        log_sum_exp(log(pi[i]),
> >                    log1m(pi[i]) - lambda[i]);
> >
> >         == log(exp(log(pi[i]))
> >                + exp(log(1 - pi[i])*exp(-lambda[i])))
> >
> >     Otherwise, everything looks OK on first glance.
> >
> >         ...
> >
> >
> >         When using Stan, I wrote R script shown below. The estimated betas are close, but truncation is ignored.
> >
> >
> >     Exactly!  This is a bug in the current version of truncation
> >     (which I'm about to fix).  It doesn't check if the
> >     values are outside the truncation range and reject.
> >
> >     I didn't think about that implementing it the first
> >     time because the right way to implement it is with
> >     the constraints.  So if you put the constraints in,
> >     it should pay attention to the constraints and do
> >     the right thing.
> >
> >      > ...
> >
> >         The estimated
> >         alphas are very different.  I must have done something wrong
> >
> >
> >     Your model should've worked as is, albeit slowly
> >     and with the danger of getting stuck outside the
> >     truncated support.
> >
> >     Version 1.0.2 should do the right thing with your
> >     existing model, but it'll be relatively slow to sample.
> >
> >     The right way to code it for 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 is with
> >     constraints.
> >
> >
> >         and would appreciate some help.  Thank you very much.
> >
> >
> >     Thanks again for letting us know and sending a detailed
> >     error report.    Please let us know if adding constraints
> >     fixes the problem.  It should.
> >
> >     - Bob
> >
> >

messages.subject: Simple latent Poisson time series model: Sampling versus Optimizing
messages.subject_clean: Simple latent Poisson time series model: Sampling versus Optimizing
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan friends,

I've been experiencing a puzzling issue trying to use Stan to fit a very simple state-space time series model with Poisson observations: whereas "sampling" with Stan works perfectly, the "optimizing" call drives the latent innovations variance (called tau in the model) to zero, despite having a rather strong prior that should keep this variance away from zero.

The attached R and Stan code reproduce the problem. Simply sourcing the "stan_sampling_vs_optim_flat.R" code in a fresh R environment will call Stan with some test data, both in sampling mode and optimizing mode, and produce a plot illustrating the issue. Note that to make the optimization somewhat "easier", I use as initial values the mean of the posterior distribution obtained after sampling, although the problem reported here is quite insensitive to initial values.

The first thing to notice is the end of the optimization trace:

initial log joint probability = 524.845
    Iter      log prob        ||dx||      ||grad||       alpha  # evals  Notes
       0       527.382     0.0607042       27.8307       0.001        2
      19       704.788      0.234647       465.337      0.2088       29
      39       879.473      0.100888       7215.49    0.000664       78
[...]
     459       1863.94     0.0145273   1.18276e+10     0.04406     1679
     479       1867.73    0.00161514   1.11964e+10      0.1327     1699
     499       1869.57    0.00274887   1.01092e+10      0.2288     1720
     519       1873.55    0.00318458   7.37747e+09      0.2044     1742
     539       1877.07    0.00691263   6.05137e+09      0.1593     1768
     559       1878.34   0.000999365   4.91358e+09           1     1789
     579       1878.85   3.32939e-05   4.07479e+09           1     1810
     595       1878.85   3.48345e-08   4.07269e+09           1     1826
Optimization terminated normally: Convergence detected: change in objective function was below tolerance

Here are the strange things:
The initial log joint probability is at a value that's typical of where MCMC finds its samples (see "lp__" in the attached density-plot and trace-plot of the MCMC sampling process).
As optimization proceeds, the log-prob increases to become very large, falling completely outside the bounds that are sampled by MCMC (which are roughly in the 450-510 range)
Also, note that the norm of the gradient becomes huge (there are some parameter range errors and gradient errors that are reported along the way, and that I did not transcribe)
At the end of the optimization, the mode of the posterior variance is close to zero:

> result.optimizing$par["tau"]
         tau
9.183124e-20

whereas the posterior distribution under MCMC is quite far from zero (again, see "tau" in the attached density-plot and trace-plot).

If all goes well, after sourcing the R file, you should see the plot attached under the name "stan_sampling_vs_optim_output.png". It shows two panels: the upper one is the raw data used to fit the model. The bottom is the posterior expectation of the Poisson process log-intensity, both under MCMC (blue curve) and the modal approximation (red curve). The latter is basically a constant and does not fit the data at all.

I have the feeling that this might be a somewhat well-known pathology, although I could not find direct references to it. Why is the log-posterior probability increasing so much during optimization, as the innovation variance is driven to zero? Where would the model specify a prior so strongly in favor of a tiny innovation variance, at the expense of the likelihood (i.e. good data fit)? I am aware of the boundary-avoiding priors described in BDA3, but I believe that my prior on tau should be sufficiently boundary-avoiding.

Any insights?

Many thanks,
+ Nicolas

messages.body_plain:
The previous version of RStan installed on the previous version of R with zero fussing, and I did cool Bayesian models quickly. Loved it.
But with  Mac OS X 10.9.3, installing RStan has been 20 miles of bad road.
The RStan Getting Started guide instructed me to create ~/.R/Makevars with exactly these two lines:
      CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++
      CXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"
This was tricky because I had to create ~/.R and to do that I had to make Mac Finder show hidden files. That was not straightforward.
The script proffered to do this does not work if ~/.R does not exist. Not having  ~/.R  was disconcerting.
Getting Started also instructed me to install Xcode 5.1.1 in order to have a C++ compiler. Some web searching revealed the trick where you run Xcode separately to accept the Apple license. And there is something about setting “Command Line Tools” in Xcode > Downloads so that refers to Xcode 5.1.1, except that seems to be Xcode > Locations, but it looks OK.
Next I updated Rcpp and inline. I also reinstalled R because I was starting to get nervous.
Then I tried the Hello World script. FAIL.
Well, it seems to run Rcpp OK, then quits at the compile stage with this message:
> Compilation argument:
> /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/bin/R CMD SHLIB file1dd173a89f7e.cpp 2> file1dd173a89f7e.cpp.err.txt
> g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++ -I/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/include -DNDEBUG  -I/usr/local/include -I/usr/local/include/freetype2 -I/opt/X11/include -I"/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.1/Resources/library/Rcpp/include"   -fPIC  "-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion" -c file1dd173a89f7e.cpp -o file1dd173a89f7e.o
> g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++ -dynamiclib -Wl,-headerpad_max_install_names -undefined dynamic_lookup -single_module -multiply_defined suppress -L/usr/local/lib -o file1dd173a89f7e.so file1dd173a89f7e.o -F/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/.. -framework R -Wl,-framework -Wl,CoreFoundation
Looks like it found Makevars OK, given the references to g++. But Xcode supplies the clang compiler. I am guessing there was no g++ so the script just ended, silently.
I seem to recall that R is compiled with clang, so now I am worrying about compatibility.
Not that I wanted to go there, but file.show("/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/etc/Makeconf") shows CC = clang and CXX = clang++.
Anyway, at this point I am forced to call for help.
Do I install g++ or should I throw away ~/.R/Makevars, ignore the Hello World test, and hope RStan works with clang?
To compile RStan, do I need g++ or is clang the right way?

My previous and positive experience with Stan led me to tell everyone where I work (fisheries research) to quit using JAGS and BUGS, so please help me get back to evangelizing Stan.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simple latent Poisson time series model: Sampling versus Optimizing
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Simple latent Poisson time series model: Sampling versus Optimizing
messages.body_plain:
> I have the feeling that this might be a somewhat well-known pathology, although I could not find direct references to it. Why is the log-posterior probability increasing so much during optimization, as the innovation variance is driven to zero? Where would the model specify a prior so strongly in favor of a tiny innovation variance, at the expense of the likelihood (i.e. good data fit)? I am aware of the boundary-avoiding priors described in BDA3, but I believe that my prior on tau should be sufficiently boundary-avoiding.

Indeed, this is a well-known pathology (but perhaps not as prevalent in the literature as it should be).

Ultimately there are two issues at play here: why do sampling and optimization behave differently,
and why is optimization falling towards the boundary at zero?  Let’s address these one at a time.

You note that you start the optimization near where the samples concentrate and then it diverges —
that is not at all unexpected.  Samples are drawn from the probability mass, which takes into
account not just the density but also the differential volume, where as optimization considers only
the density.  Consequently the neighborhood where samples concentrate (what we call the typical
set) will not, in general, be close to the posterior maximum.  In fact the posterior maximum doesn’t
even have a strong mathematical motivation [1].

If you plot the posterior density for the innovation variance verses its dependent variables
you should see a funnel-like structure, with the high density towards zero variance concentrating
in a very narrow volume.  This narrow volume disfavors the zero-variance region when sampling,
which is why the samples appear so much better behaved.

Okay, so maybe the samples and the optimum shouldn’t be all that similar, but why is the optimum
diverging?  The problem is that although you’re adding regularizing prior information it is nowhere
near strong enough.  In models like this the likelihood dominates all but the strongest, unrealistic
prior information.  I don’t think I’ve ever seen a hierarchical model where the hyper variances didn’t
have maxima at the boundary, but that’s okay because I never try to optimize.  :-)

One thing you can do is reparameterize — if you optimize to log variance you should see a maximum
displaced from the boundary [2].

[1] The terse answer I would like to give is “don’t EVER optimize a density, because it doesn’t
mean anything mathematically”.  These kinds of pathologies are just manifestations of this
underlying principle.

[2] The fact that the maximum depends on the (arbitrary) parameterization is a good sign that
something is wrong with the maximum.

messages.body_plain:
>
> Many thanks for your reply and suggestions. I agree that one should avoid blindly optimizing if at all possible, but sometimes it is necessary... Your reparametrization idea indeed solves the problem: modeling the log-variance produces a well-behaved optimization.
>
> My original problem (not posted) arose from a hierarchical model with a similar time-series structure — I will see if your insights help me avoid the same variance collapse problem.
>
> A more philosophical question: your point [1] says  “don’t EVER optimize a density, because it doesn’t mean anything mathematically”. But isn't where maximum likelihood comes from in the first place? [Not that I would find it unusual that a card-carrying Bayesian should find MLE meaningless :-) ]

This is going to become necessarily mathematical (also super Bayesian) and so apologies
in advance for the technical nature of the response.

Firstly, what are we really manipulating when we talk about probabilities?  Probability
densities aren’t really all that fundamental: the fundamental object is something called
a probability measure that assigns probabilities to well-behaved collections of events.
Probability measures exist to be integrated, in other words they provide a way of
computing expectations like means, variances, and quantiles.  Concepts like “most
probably event” are not well defined.

Now probability measures are abstract objects that live in abstract spaces, but with a
choice of parameterization they can be mapped into the real numbers, and that mapping
provides the probability densities with which most people are familiar.  These densities,
however, are only a convenience meant to ease the computation of expectations with
respect to the underlying measure.  Other properties like optima have no real meaning [1].

One reason optima are ill-defined is that they depend on the arbitrary parameterization
used in defining the densities.  When you report a MAP estimator you are adding additional
(often implicit) assumptions!  Note that expectations computed with the densities, however,
do not depend on the parameterization as the integral of a density is an invariant object.

What does this imply for statistics?  That depends on how you interpret uncertainty.

>From a Bayesian perspective everything is a random variable, and we can apply Bayes’
Theorem to construct a posterior measure.  In practice we define a parameterization of
the model space which gives us a posterior density with which it is easier to compute.
But we have to need to heed the warning above and not try to do something foolish like
optimize in complicated models.

The Frequentist perspective is completely different.  Here only the data is random
and we don’t have a single posterior measure over the model space but rather a family
of measures defined over the data space.  This likelihood function defines a measure
over the data for every choice of model (value of the parameters) and one builds
expectations over the data that attempt to estimate the underlying model.  Taking
expectations over the data space gives functions, not densities, like E[x] ( \theta )
which can readily be optimized to give Frequentist estimators, estimators whose
utility strongly depends on how much you believe in the Frequentist perspective.

In simple cases [1] Bayesian expectations and Frequentist estimators like the MLE
appear to be similar, and this lulls people into make claims like “Bayes is just
Frequentist estimators with regularization”.  But this is a very naive perspective
and doesn't generalize to the complex systems common in modern applied statistics!

[1] There can be coincidences, however.  For some measures in some parameterizations,
such as the standard Normal distribution, the maximum of the density coincides with
the mean and the maximum appears to have some computational use.  Indeed if you can
show that an optimum in a given parameterization approximates a mean then it can
provide a useful approximation.  In practice, however, this is limited to simple models
like the exponential family in few dimensions, which are rare in real applications.

I'm sorry to say we don't have anything on the GUI front yet.

The standard Bayesian approach to inference is to jointly
model and estimate all the variables --- it's the only sound
way to do inference in most cases.  Breaking apart problems
and communicating through samples or estimates is usually
a last computational resort for problems that are too big
to deal with otherwise.

- Bob

messages.subject: A function that allows you to run a stan model and it automatically checks if it's been compiled
messages.subject_clean: A function that allows you to run a stan model and it automatically checks if it's been compiled
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  We have no gui yet but in an upcoming release of rstan we will be allowing simple model reuse.  Just use the following code that was supplied to us by Sebastian Weber.  First create this function:

stan_run <- function(stanModel, ...) {
  stanModel.rda <- gsub("stan$", "rda", stanModel)
  if(!file.exists(stanModel.rda) || file.info <http://file.info>(stanModel.rda)$mtime < file.info <http://file.info>(stanModel)$mtime) {
    cat("Model needs compilation.\n")
    args <- modifyList(list(...), list(file=stanModel, iter=0, warmup=0, chains=0))
    stanExe <- do.call(stan, args)
    save(stanExe, file=stanModel.rda)
  } else {
    cat("Loading cached model.\n")
    load(stanModel.rda)
  }
  stan(fit=stanExe, ...)
}

Then you can run a stan model using stan_run with the file name, for example:

fit_full <- stan_run (“ep_hierarchical_logistic.stan", data=list (N=fake$N, J=fake$J, K=fake$K, jj=fake$jj, X=fake$X, y=fake$y, mu_0=mu_0, Sigma_0=Sigma_0), iter=1000, chains=4)

The first time it runs it will compile the model and save the compiled model in your working directory.  On future runs it uses the compiled version.  But it checks the date of the model file, and if you alter it, it automatically knows to recompile.  Much more convenient than having to save R workspaces.  Also it works fine when you shut down R or turn off the computer or whatever.

A

However, there is something worrying about making it 'too easy' to use, old arguments we have heard 1000 times before about SPSS and goodness knows what else. messages.subject: Matrix exponential
messages.subject_clean: Matrix exponential
messages.body_plain:
I think it'd be lovely to have matrix exponentials in Stan.   I would use this for continuous-time Markov models.  I know it's notoriously hard to calculate, but JAGS has a module for it (using Pade approximation) and the "expm" R package has a variety of algorithms, with a C API.   Not sure about calculating the derivatives, I suspect it would be difficult if the matrix is not diagonalizable - though in the class of models I'd use it for, it generally would be.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
The problem is indeed in the derivatives — unless the matrix is symmetric the derivatives
of the matrix exponential are either ill-defined or very hard to compute.  The first order
derivatives have actually been computed for Riemannian HMC but they are a mess, and
likely won’t be incorporated into a matrix_exp function anytime soon.

If you add this as a feature request at https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues then it
won’t get lost in the mailing list, but no promises on when it might ever be implemented.

messages.subject: Rstan manual multivariate hierarchical regression example: row_vector problem in multi_normal
messages.subject_clean: Rstan manual multivariate hierarchical regression example: row_vector problem in multi_normal
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I am trying to recreate the multivariate regression example from page 92 (section 9.9) in the most recent Rstan manual, as it fits the type of analysis that I want to run on a psychological experiment.

My goal is to adjust the subject level data (‘groups’) that I have with the population/group-level predictors. Each subject undertakes 22 trials in a decision-making task, with binary responses. Hence I am using a linear regression model at the group level and a logistic function at the subject level.

My problem is that I am running into a well-documented problem: I am creating a row-vector in line 27 when multiplying the group predictors (u[s]) with gamma. the multi-normal function only accepts vectors as inputs:

Error in stanc("GBE_hierarchical_logistic_linear.stan") :

  failed to parse Stan model 'GBE_hierarchical_logistic_linear' with error message:

EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=27, column=56

    beta[s] ~ multi_normal((u[s] * gamma), Sigma_beta);

                                                       ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

no matches for function name="multi_normal_log"

    arg 0 type=vector

    arg 1 type=row vector

    arg 2 type=matrix

available function signatures for multi_normal_log:

0.  multi_normal_log(vector, vector, matrix) : real

unknown distribution=multi_normal

Parser expecting: <eps>

I simulated data to test this model. The simulated data is structured as follows: 50 subjects, three parameters to be estimated per subject, two group predictors, each subject's true parameters are drawn from a normal distribution, with non-zero mean and std. of 3.

My questions:

1. Since I have exactly recreated the example rstan code given on page 95; I wonder whether I made a mistake or whether the example as described in the manual cannot currently be run in rstan given the row_vector restriction in the multi_normal function.

2. As my data has to be structured the way it is set up, I wonder whether there is a work around for me? I saw that the issue (#589) is fixed on the development platform.

Please find attached my stan code; a matlab file that simulates data; the matlab data output (mat file); the code that runs the rstan model. Note that R.matlab has to be installed to read the mat file into R.

For some reason the file upload isn't working, here's a dropbox link: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/hx7gqkcy3b3sjah/AACIyOcjzXmNY76Xx89d0mf4a

Thank you very much for your help in advance!

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for looking for answers and sorry the list is so hard
to search!

For now, the simplest thing to do is transpose (postfix ' operator),
so you'd use:

  beta[s]' ~ multi_normal((u[s] * gamma), Sigma_beta);

A more efficient alternative would to be declare beta as
an array of vectors (I'm not actually sure what M and N
should be in your case --- this assumes beta was declared as
an M x N matrix).

   vector[N] beta[M];

There's a discussion of vectors/matrices vs. arrays and efficiency
in a chapter of the manual.

The generalization and vectorization of multi_normal hasn't
been merged into develop yet, but it's going to be soon and
will be in the next release, 2.3.0, which we hope to get out later
this week or early next week.

Here's the issue and pull request to track:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/589

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/608

When Marco's fix is merged, your original code will work as written.

- Bob

Hey all,

I just wanted to alert the list that I just installed RStan on a new Mac (Mavericks, latest Xcode) and had a similar problem to Fredrik and Sam compiling the 8 schools code . I followed the instructions on the RStan Getting Started page and had R crash on me when I tried to run the 8 schools example. I followed Ben's instructions above to reinstall Rcpp and inline (copy/pasted Ben's above into the R console) from source, and the 8 schools code now runs fine. Given that a few other users have had similar problems, I wonder if there is a versioning issue with what R installs when install.packages(c('Rcpp','inline')) is called vs. install.packages(c('Rcpp', 'inline'), type = 'source').

Rob

  for (n in 1:N_obs)
    y[n] ~ categorical_logit(beta);

messages.subject: Regular (non-normalized) incomplete gamma function?
messages.subject_clean: Regular (non-normalized) incomplete gamma function?
messages.body_plain:
I have an unusual estimation problem that requires evaluating the expression:

log( lambda*( exp(-lambda*y) - lambda*y*Gamma(0,lambda*y) ) )

where Gamma(a,z) is the typical incomplete gamma function (from z to infinity).

The expression above is the solution to an integral that averages over uncertainty in a certain kind of censored exponential. The trouble is that Stan seems to have only normalized incomplete gamma functions. I've tried a few series approximations, but numerical issues are making it pretty unreliable.

Looks like what I need is tgamma(a,z) from Boost: http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_35_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/special/sf_gamma/igamma.html

Any ideas for how to approach this? Should I wait for tgamma(a,z) to get added in?

Btw, this is a small component of a larger hidden Markov model I've coded in Stan. The forward algorithm code in the manual helped me get that going right away. Thanks for the clear example. Every other piece of the model is working very smoothly.

messages.body_plain:
Seems like there's some crosstalk here.

The parser isn't the problem. The problem is that the transpose symbol is a single quote ' instead of the slanted accent symbol  ´.

But since you quoted your model code within single quote marks, you can't use a single quote mark within the model code.

To fix this, just use double quotes " to enclose your model code. Then replace the ´ with ' for the transposition.

Do you want zeroes so that it's not full rank and only positive
semi-definite?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Good catch.

The problem with the mu parameter with no distribution
specified is that Stan treats it as uniform on (-infinity, infinity),
which leads to an improper posterior.  Stan requires proper
posteriors to sample.    One way to guarantee this is with proper
priors, but Stan can handle improper priors as long as the posterior
is proper.  There's a chapter discussing why such posteriors are
problematic in the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Post-processing of Stan results to get frequentist p-values
messages.subject_clean: Post-processing of Stan results to get frequentist p-values
messages.body_plain:
Included is code to post-process Stan results to get frequentist p-values for the sampled parameters, e.g., with a likelihood-ratio test. "mcmc4" is an example with a normal distribution. "mcmc6" is an example with a negative binomial distribution.

Currently, a large part is implemented in R. However the implementation does nothing what Stan doesn't do anyway (sampling, simulation, minimization, importance sampling). Any idea how to let Stan do more of the work?

Best regards,

Christian

P.S.
The implemented algorithm is an extension of
- Harrison, Matthew T. "Conservative hypothesis tests and confidence intervals using importance sampling." Biometrika 99.1 (2012): 57-69.
and is described in
- Bartels, Christian (2014): Efficient generic integration algorithm to determine confidence intervals and p-values for hypothesis testing. figshare.
http://dx.doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.1054694

To answer your literal question:  You can assign individual int
values to real variables. So you could define a matrix and then
assign it:

  int foo[I,J];
  matrix[I,J] bar;
  for (i in 1:I)
    for (j in 1:J)
      bar[i,j] <- foo[i,j];

But I somehow doubt this is what you want to be doing anyway.
Why would you multiply probabilities by states in an HMM
implementation?

Don't worry about bothering us with questions.  Well, maybe
a little bit --- we don't have infinite amounts of time.  But
it's important for us to hear where people are getting confused.
And we'd rather help than just frustrate our users.  And then
hopefully make things clearer.

On Jun 14, 2014, at 7:08 PM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:

>

>

>
> I think I should be using the following likelihood
> for(tm in 2:Ntime){
> State[tm]~multinomial(TransMatrix * State[tm-1]);
>
> }
>

Stan has both a categorical distribution and a multinomial,
and you almost certainly want the categorical for this (single integer
outcome) and not the multinomial (vector of counts outcome).

Look at the signatures in the index of the manual and then look at
the definitions to make sure you're using the right distribution.

> Where state is a integer vector, TransMatrix is a 3x3 matrix... but then what do I do about State[tm-1].... I can't do integer by matrix multiplication. Should I have 2 variables for state, one integer and one vector? or is there a trick I could use with the categorical distribution? Really hoping for some advice.

Yes, you need to either do the matrix multiplication by hand in a loop,
or assign the integer values to a matrix and then use matrix multiplication.

I still don't understand why you'd want to matrix multiply states,
but I thought I'd at least answer your literal question.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Is the goal of that matrix multiplication just to get the transition probabilities corresponding to previsious State? For example, if State[tm-1]==2, you would like to get row number 2 from TransMatrix? The problem is that it actually return column 2, I can't see how that could be what you want.

That being said, I think it would be much cleaner to use categorical distribution directly instead of multinomial. But it requires a couple of changes to the original code. The main thing is that instead of of representing the State as a vector of length three we use just integers (ie. State==1 or State==2 or State==3).

I have attached edited version of the model to this post. In addition of that change of the distribution, I added parameter TAU to the parameter list (and give it a prior distribution) and changed the data generation accordingly. Did you want to have 5 patients&52 datapoints or just one? If more than one, change the State to integer array etc.

Edit: Didn't noticed at first, but the transformed parameters part of the model doesn't always produce matrix with row sums of exactly 1. Is there any particular reason to use that particular parametrization, or would it be possible to use something else, like softmax?

messages.body_plain:
The problem is that the variance parameters sigmas aren't constrained to the corresponding uniform intervals. Ie. the samper will generate sigma's from the interval [0,Inf] and then if sigma[k] > uppersigma[k] the sampling statement uniform(0,uppersigma[k]) will increase the log-posterior by -Infinity.

So I think there are two possibilies:
a) use different prior as Andrew suggested
b) declare 4 sigmas in the form of real<lower=0,upper=uppersigma> sigma

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stanfolk,

I'm using rstan to fit a non-linear regression model that considers measurement error in both dependent and independent variables. The model compiles and runs fine, as long as I specify rstan to just produce one chain (the results look entirely plausible, see example fit to data in attached pdf).

However, when I tell rstan to run multiple chains, R always successfully completes the first chain, but then beeps, scrolls to the top of the gui output, and freezes (scrolling still possible, but not typing/copy/pasting). Sometimes some sampling of the second chain seems to occur before R freezes in this way. There are no informative error messages, apart from regular metropolis rejections of initial values of the first, and sometimes, second chain.

I've attached an .r file that generates data, fits the model, and freezes upon initialization of the second chain.

I've retried de-installing rstan, installing inline and rcpp from source, and re-installing rstan, but to no avail. I've also tried rerunning things with subsets of packages loaded, and on one occasion the second chain was successfully simulated when plyr wasn't loaded, although it failed again on repeated attempts (lucky shot?). Below is my session info.

Thanks,

Luc

On Jun 15, 2014, at 4:13 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi, Franzi.  I just have a couple comments.  First, as Bob C. knows, I really don’t like uniform priors (except for parameters with natural constraints such as correlations which are bounded between -1 and 1).  I much prefer soft constraints to hard constraints, both for computational and statistical reasons (the folk theorem comes in here).  Second, I don’t see why there would be a problem to fit 4 regression models in one go.  You just have to define all 4 sets of parameters in the model.
> A
>
> On Jun 15, 2014, at 6:01 AM, f ko <fraenzi...@oikostat.ch> wrote:
>
>> Dears
>> I would like to fit 4 different regression lines to the same data. Each regression line has a different prior for the sigma parameter:
>> Uniform(0,uppersigma)
>> with uppersigma being 5, 10, 50, and 1000
>> The true sigma is 5. My aim is to show 4 histograms of the 4 posterior distributions of sigma. From this plot we should see that the posterior based on the prior Unif(0,5) is constraint, whereas we get nice posterior distributions when the upper limit of the prior is larger than the upper tail of the posterior.
>>
>> When I use uppersigma=c(10, 20, 50, 1000), I get a good fit for all 4 models, but the 4 posteriors for sigma look very similar... When I specify one of the uppersigma-values to be lower than 8, so that it constrains the posterior of sigma, the fit of ALL 4 models becomes very bad (very low neffs, high Rhat values) and all 4 posteriors for sigma are bimodal with one mass close to zero and the other mass close to the uppersigma value.  Obviously, the choice of the uppersigma for one regression line influences the fit of all the other regression lines, even if (I think) I specified 4 independent regression lines (model code below).
>>
>> Isn't it possible to fit 4 independent regression lines to the same data in one go?
>> Before, I fitted 20 independent regression lines with different priors for the slope parameter and this seemed to work nicely. But maybe this was wrong too?
>> The R-Code to simulate the data and fit the model below using rstan is attached.
>> Thanks in advance!
>> Fränzi
>>
>>
>> // Normal linear regressions with varying
>> // priors for sigma to assess
>> // the influence of the prior for sigma
>>
>> data {
>>   int<lower=0> n;
>>   vector[n] y;
>>   vector[n] x;
>>   vector[4] uppersigma;
>> }
>> parameters {
>>   vector[4] beta0;
>>   vector[4] beta1;
>>   real<lower=0> sigma[4];
>> }
>> model {
>>   //priors
>>   beta0 ~ normal(0,10);
>>   beta1 ~ normal(0,10);
>>   for(k in 1:4){
>>     sigma[k] ~ uniform(0,uppersigma[k]);
>>     // likelihood
>>     y ~ normal(beta0[k] + beta1[k] * x, sigma[k]);
>>   }
>> }
>>

messages.body_plain:
The most efficient thing to use for a single draw is
categorical_logit.  Unfortunately, that has a memory leak
in Stan 2.2 that's fixed for 2.3, which should be out soon.

Until then, I'd suggest just using exp(alpha) / sum(alpha)
to implement softmax and plug into the categorical distribution.

And when you say it's slow, I'm curious how it compares to JAGS
in terms of convergence and mixing speed (wall time to convergence
and number of effective samples per time unit after convergence).
(Just counting iterations isn't useful to compare different MCMC
algorithms.)

- Bob

No --- alpha should be the regression values on the unconstrained

  softmax(alpha) =def= exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha))

Sorry --- I missed the exp(alpha) on the first one.

So you want to do this with a local variable for exp(alpha), as in:

  vector[K] alpha;

  {

    simplex[K] softmax_alpha;
    exp_alpha <- exp(alpha);
    softmax_alpha <- exp_alpha / sum(exp_alpha);

variables.  If you want to save softmax_alpha, declare it as

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Post-processing of Stan results to get frequentist p-values
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Post-processing of Stan results to get frequentist p-values
messages.body_plain:
I don't really know either R or hypothesis testing well enough
to help here.  Just a few points:

1.  Stan can only operate on one iteration at a time.  Look
at the generated quantities block for making computations based
on data and params on a per-iteration basis.  So as soon as you
create 'par' and operate on columns at a time, you're beyond what
you can currently do within Stan itself.

2.  You have to be careful with MCMC output, as you want to
divide by n_eff, not n in any hypothesis tests due to the correlation
of the posterior.

3.  You use an improper p(sigma) propto 1/sigma prior.  This is OK,
as is a general improper uniform prior, as long as the posterior is
proper.

4.  Renaming is error prone --- I'd suggest just making the model match
whatever you do with it other than renaming.

If you have further questions about specific Stan capabilities,
we'd be happy to help.

- Bob

On Jun 14, 2014, at 6:44 AM, Christian Bartels <hanschrist...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Included is code to post-process Stan results to get frequentist p-values for the sampled parameters, e.g., with a likelihood-ratio test. "mcmc4" is an example with a normal distribution. "mcmc6" is an example with a negative binomial distribution.
>
> Currently, a large part is implemented in R. However the implementation does nothing what Stan doesn't do anyway (sampling, simulation, minimization, importance sampling). Any idea how to let Stan do more of the work?
>
> Best regards,
>
> Christian
>
> P.S.
> The implemented algorithm is an extension of
> - Harrison, Matthew T. "Conservative hypothesis tests and confidence intervals using importance sampling." Biometrika 99.1 (2012): 57-69.
> and is described in
> - Bartels, Christian (2014): Efficient generic integration algorithm to determine confidence intervals and p-values for hypothesis testing. figshare.
> http://dx.doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.1054694
>
>

messages.body_plain:
softmax is the inverse link function for multi-logistic
GLMs.

softmax maps arbitrary points alpha in R^K into K-simplexes
(i.e., K-vectors with non-negative vectors that sum to 1).
A K-simplex is the parameter to a categorical (or multinomial)
distribution.  It's also the support for a K-dimensional Dirichlet
distribution.

I don't know what a "transition intensity" is.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Dear STAN team,

I am recently learning to use STAN. There is a classic Theophylline example in NONMEM, so I just want to redo it in STAN. But a couple of problems arise, so I really need your help.

Background:
We have 12 subjects, each with 11 observations.
theta1 ,theta2, theta3 are fixed effects.
eta1, eta2, eta3 are random effects with mean 0.
sigma is the error term and Omega is the covariance matrix.

I want to have the estimates of 3 fixed effects, 1 error term and 6 covariance parameters and code are in newtest.stan.

Problems are:
1. If I specify Omega as cov_matrix[3], I got 3 kinds of the messages: (1) Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is inf:0, but must be finite! (2) Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_prec_log(d): LDLT_Factor of precision parameterunderlying matrix is not positive definite. LDLT_Factor of precision parameterlast conditional variance is 180.4616997051736. and (3) Optimization terminated with error:  Line search failed to achieve a sufficient decrease, no more progress can be made
The result in output.csv is not in accordance with NONMEM output

2. If I specify Omega as matrix[3,3], I got the message: Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_prec_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Precision matrixPrecision matrix is not symmetric. Precision matrix[1,2] is -14.756310354014762:0, but Precision matrix[2,1] element is -14.7563:0
Optimization terminated normally:  Convergence detected: change in objective function was below tolerance
Even though it is converged, but result in output.csv is not in accordance with NONMEM output

Question:
Did I make some mistakes or Could you please give me some suggestions?

Thank you so much!

Bests,
Fei

PS: theo5.nmctl.txt is the NONMEM file and theo5.ext.txt is the NONMEM output

messages.subject: Model design: detect latent temporal change points in regression parameters
messages.subject_clean: Model design: detect latent temporal change points in regression parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I’m here to ask for some guidance with design of a model that detects latent temporal change points in regression parameters. I’ve been dabbling with RStan for a few months and am really impressed with the documentation and support, but as a novice Bayesian I’ve run into a sticking point that, with any luck, will be trivial to someone more experienced.

tl;dr - looking for Stan approach to infer step-change of regression parameters before and after a latent temporal change point.

The simple case I’ll use for illustration is univariate linear regression of response variable y as a function of predictor x, which is a random variable drawn once per time step from a normal distribution N(.) . There is also a Gaussian noise term in the response, with standard deviation sig_y.

y = a + b*x + noise —> y ~ N(a + b*x, sig_y)

x ~ N(.)

Could hardly be simpler. In the system under study, there is reason to believe that the system undergoes a step change in functional response, and thus regression parameters, at some change point time Tcp, such that:

y ~ N(a[1] + b[1]*x, sig_y)   for t <= Tcp

y ~ N(a[2] + b[2]*x, sig_y)  for t >   Tcp

My objective is to infer Tcp, a[1:2], and b[1:2].

As posed, Tcp is discrete and thus can’t be directly represented in Stan. I implemented a hack solution in Stan that just pretends Tcp is continuous, which essentially treats any value of Tcp between time steps as equally likely. This actually works sometimes (meaning it converges and correctly estimates synthetic data parameters) but other times it fails badly (doesn’t converge, incorrect inference). I imagine this abuse of parameters has any number of undesirable consequences.

I've attached the Stan code for this hack, as well as synthetic data (n=80, true parameters: Tcp=48, a[1] = 0, b[1] = 1, a[2] = 1, b[2] = 0.5, sig_y = 0.5) and the R code for generating random data.

The manual and other discussions recommend “summing out” latent variables for mixing problems, but this isn’t really a mixing problem because the grouping is a deterministic function of Tcp, and anyway Tcp is the sought parameter. For this phase of my analysis I would be happy to estimate Tcp alone, and perhaps if I were more clever it would be obvious how to sum out the other parameters and end up with a continuous representation of the change point. But so far I’m not that clever.

Many Thanks,

-Thomas

Note:

My actual model is considerably more complicated, accounting for multiple error sources following the hierarchical approach described in

Kelly, B. C. (2007), Some Aspects of Measurement Error in Linear Regression of Astronomical Data, Astrophys. J., 665(2), 1489, doi:10.1086/519947.

and extended to a constrained segmented linear model that is applied to hydrologic data with threshold behavior. The approach works well for lumped data (no temporal change points), but the small successes I’ve had with estimating Tcp for the simplified example above entirely fail for the more complex model.

Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin10.8.0 (64-bit)

built with the GNU standard library (libstdc++).  g++ defaults to libstdc++, which is why the easiest fix
is to install RStan with g++ and then switch back to Clang for the improved model compilation.  Alternatively
one can always install using Clang but forcing -lib=libstdc++.

The conflict that’s causing RStan compilation to fail with libc++ has been fixed and will be available in
the forthcoming RStan2.3.

messages.subject: Re: Model design: detect latent temporal change points in regression parameters
messages.subject_clean: Model design: detect latent temporal change points in regression parameters
messages.body_plain:
Although your hack may seem to work (sometimes), the posterior you're simulating is not smooth anymore because you are treating Tcp with a step-function. This causes a discontinuity in the posterior wherever the sampler crosses a value of Tcp that is also present in the dataset.

Solution: summing out things after all. What you need to sum out are all possible relevant values of Tcp. I.e., if in your dataset you have observations at time 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, you need to marginalize out over the unobserved values of Tcp > 1 Tcp <= 2, Tcp > 2 Tcp <= 3, Tcp > 3 Tcp <= 4, Tcp > 4 Tcp <= 5, and Tcp > 5 Tcp <= 6. In other words, you won't ever be able to estimate the exact value of Tcp, as it is interval censored. You can however estimate in which interval Tcp is most likely to be, given the intervals at which you observe the data.

Luc

messages.subject: Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.subject_clean: Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm finally getting to grips with GPs, and am now looking at the
multivariate case for application to my real-world data. Specifically,
I deal with EEG data where we get measure voltage as a function of
time and position on the skull. Taking a simple spherical model of the
skull, we can encode position in terms of longitude and latitude (or
phi & theta if you want to use polar coordinates). I see from the
example in the manual how to combine two variables where simple
euclidean distance is computed, i.e. (pg 144):

     data {
       int<lower=1> D;
       int<lower=1> N;
       vector[D] x[N];
     }
     transformed data {
     ...
           Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-dot_self(x[i] - x[j]))
                         + if_else(i==j, 0.1, 0.0);
     ...

Any ideas on how to do this with one simple continuous variate (time)
and spherical coordinates?

Also, if I move to a fitting/inference context where I evaluate the GP
hyperparamters (eta, sigma, rho), presumably something should be done
to reflect the fact that time and spatial coordinates are very
different metrics and therefore might have different best-suited
hyperparameter values, no? The obvious solution would be to have two
additive GPs, one for time and one for the spherical coordinate, and
thus two sets of GP hyperparameters, but I don't want to assume that
the same temporal function exists at all spatial coordinates and vice
versa. Any thoughts?

Thanks in advance,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

I think the answer you are looking for is in the Stan manual, section "Automatic Relevance Detection" (p.147 of the Stan 2.2.0 manual). It basically boils down to allowing rho to vary by dimension. In your case, the two values of rho pertaining to space would be the same, and the third value of rho pertaining to time would be allowed to be estimated separately. Your suggestion of using two additive GPs would mean you would also allow eta to vary between time and space. I'm not sure whether this is necessary; it would add an extra parameter to the model that you might not need.

messages.body_plain:
What Luc says! And the reason it doesn't work well is that
HMC doesn't deal with discontinuity --- it's following
gradients and resorts to a poor random walk (based solely
on the random momentum) if the function's not differentiable.

The marginalization is possible, but may not be very efficient if
the number of time steps is large.  You'll need to create a vector
of the log probs from each choice and use log_sum_exp as in the
mixture chapter of the manual.  On the other hand, other
methods are also not likely to be very efficient at this, either.
For instance, you'd need the same sort of computation to do Gibbs.

- Bob

On Jun 19, 2014, at 5:23 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Although your hack may seem to work (sometimes), the posterior your simulating is not smooth anymore because you are treating Tcp with a step-function. This causes a discontinuity in the posterior wherever the sampler crosses a value of Tcp that is also present in the dataset.

>
> Solution: summing out things after all. What you need to sum out are all possible relevant values of Tcp. I.e., if in your dataset you have observations at time 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, you need to marginalize out over the unobserved values of Tcp > 1 Tcp <= 2, Tcp > 2 Tcp <= 3, Tcp > 3 Tcp <= 4, Tcp > 4 Tcp <= 5, and Tcp > 5 Tcp <= 6. In other words, you won't ever be able to estimate the exact value of Tcp, as it is interval censored. You can however estimate in which interval Tcp is most likely to be, given the intervals at which you observe the data.
>
> Luc
>

>
> I’m here to ask for some guidance with design of a model that detects latent temporal change points in regression parameters. I’ve been dabbling with RStan for a few months and am really impressed with the documentation and support, but as a novice Bayesian I’ve run into a sticking point that, with any luck, will be trivial to someone more experienced.
>
> tl;dr - looking for Stan approach to infer step-change of regression parameters before and after a latent temporal change point.
>
> The simple case I’ll use for illustration is univariate linear regression of response variable y as a function of predictor x, which is a random variable drawn once per time step from a normal distribution N(.) . There is also a Gaussian noise term in the response, with standard deviation sig_y.
>
> y = a + b*x + noise —> y ~ N(a + b*x, sig_y)
>
> x ~ N(.)
>
> Could hardly be simpler. In the system under study, there is reason to believe that the system undergoes a step change in functional response, and thus regression parameters, at some change point time Tcp, such that:
>
> y ~ N(a[1] + b[1]*x, sig_y)  for t <= Tcp
>
> y ~ N(a[2] + b[2]*x, sig_y) for t >   Tcp
>
> My objective is to infer Tcp, a[1:2], and b[1:2].
>
> As posed, Tcp is discrete and thus can’t be directly represented in Stan. I implemented a hack solution in Stan that just pretends Tcp is continuous, which essentially treats any value of Tcp between time steps as equally likely. This actually works sometimes (meaning it converges and correctly estimates synthetic data parameters) but other times it fails badly (doesn’t converge, incorrect inference). I imagine this abuse of parameters has any number of undesirable consequences.

messages.body_plain:
It's more efficient  to write

  gamma ~ normal(1,1);

and rely on the vectorization.  Using multi_normal is relatively
inefficient.

And we really need to rewrite some of those models.  Using exp(log_gamma)
is a bad idea.  If you're going to make something positive, it's
cleaner to just declare the variable as:

  vector<lower=0>[K] gamma;

Rather than having a log_gamma without a constraint and then exponentiating.
Then the lower-bound constraint takes care of the exponentiation in
the background for you.

Identifiability in theory is not the same as in practice.  In practice,
it may take a lot of samples to read convergence if a parameter is
not well identified in the posterior.  So cranking down one of the
parameters to normal(0,1) will identify the scale.

- Bob

It basically boils down to allowing rho to vary by dimension. In your case, the two values of rho pertaining to space would be the same, and the third value of rho pertaining to time would be allowed to be estimated separately. Your suggestion of using two additive GPs would mean you would also allow eta to vary between time and space. I'm not sure whether this is necessary; it would add an extra parameter to the model that you might not need.

On Wednesday, June 18, 2014 7:50:04 PM UTC-7, Thomas Moran wrote:
>
> Hi everyone,
>
> I’m here to ask for some guidance with design of a model that detects latent temporal change points in regression parameters. I’ve been dabbling with RStan for a few months and am really impressed with the documentation and support, but as a novice Bayesian I’ve run into a sticking point that, with any luck, will be trivial to someone more experienced.
>
> tl;dr - looking for Stan approach to infer step-change of regression parameters before and after a latent temporal change point.
>
> The simple case I’ll use for illustration is univariate linear regression of response variable y as a function of predictor x, which is a random variable drawn once per time step from a normal distribution N(.) . There is also a Gaussian noise term in the response, with standard deviation sig_y.
>
> y = a + b*x + noise —> y ~ N(a + b*x, sig_y)
>
> x ~ N(.)
>
> Could hardly be simpler. In the system under study, there is reason to believe that the system undergoes a step change in functional response, and thus regression parameters, at some change point time Tcp, such that:
>
> y ~ N(a[1] + b[1]*x, sig_y)   for t <= Tcp
>
> y ~ N(a[2] + b[2]*x, sig_y)  for t >   Tcp
>
> My objective is to infer Tcp, a[1:2], and b[1:2].
>
> As posed, Tcp is discrete and thus can’t be directly represented in Stan. I implemented a hack solution in Stan that just pretends Tcp is continuous, which essentially treats any value of Tcp between time steps as equally likely. This actually works sometimes (meaning it converges and correctly estimates synthetic data parameters) but other times it fails badly (doesn’t converge, incorrect inference). I imagine this abuse of parameters has any number of undesirable consequences.
>
> I've attached the Stan code for this hack, as well as synthetic data (n=80, true parameters: Tcp=48, a[1] = 0, b[1] = 1, a[2] = 1, b[2] = 0.5, sig_y = 0.5) and the R code for generating random data.
>
> The manual and other discussions recommend “summing out” latent variables for mixing problems, but this isn’t really a mixing problem because the grouping is a deterministic function of Tcp, and anyway Tcp is the sought parameter. For this phase of my analysis I would be happy to estimate Tcp alone, and perhaps if I were more clever it would be obvious how to sum out the other parameters and end up with a continuous representation of the change point. But so far I’m not that clever.
>
> Many Thanks,
>
> -Thomas
>
>
> Note:
>
> My actual model is considerably more complicated, accounting for multiple error sources following the hierarchical approach described in
>
> Kelly, B. C. (2007), Some Aspects of Measurement Error in Linear Regression of Astronomical Data, Astrophys. J., 665(2), 1489, doi:10.1086/519947.
>
> and extended to a constrained segmented linear model that is applied to hydrologic data with threshold behavior. The approach works well for lumped data (no temporal change points), but the small successes I’ve had with estimating Tcp for the simplified example above entirely fail for the more complex model.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can Stan do mixed membership?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can Stan do mixed membership?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the response Bob. I guess I'm using terminology used by the folks at Bristol. The paper that has what I'm interested in is here: http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20130401151715/http://www.education.gov.uk/publications/eorderingdownload/rr791.pdf

Mixed membership model is a multilevel model in which units belong to multiple groups of the same type. For example, a firm might operate in multiple countries with known weights (summing to 1).

Weighted variance components model is just the terminology the Bristol guys are using for a multilevel model in which the random group effect is weighted by the known weights mentioned above.

Level 2 predictors are just group-level predictors.

I haven't seen this implemented in BUGS or JAGS. It seems that they use MLwiN.

On Thursday, June 19, 2014 9:35:40 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On Jun 19, 2014, at 2:05 PM, Christopher Grainger <cigra...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > I've been looking to implement a mixed membership model (e.g. students across multiple schools or firms operating in multiple countries) and I'm wondering if it's possible to estimate weighted variance components models with Stan. There do not appear to be any implementations in the existing examples. Has anyone done this before? Is it possible? With Level 2 predictors?
>
> I don't know what any of these are:
>
>   * mixed membership model
>
>   * weighted variance components models
>
>   * level 2 predictors
>
>
> If you can write down the joint density of data and parameters
> and all the parameters are continuous, then you can probably fit
> in Stan.
>
> Are there examples in BUGS or JAGS?  If so, they're usually
> pretty easy to translate (unless you have to marginalize discrete
> parameters).
>
> For what it's worth, we're going to be spending a lot of
> time over the next two or three years working on a range
> of education models.   So we're quite interested in
> coverage here if we can understand the models.
>
> - Bob

But so far I’m not that clever.

What would be wrong with a continuous time and modelling by y~a+log(e^(S*k1*(x_Tcp))/(1+e^(S*k2*(x-Tcp))))/S+\epsilon ? This is smooth, has slopes k1 for x<<Tcp, k1-k2 for x>>Tcp and the junction of the two segments becomes sharper with increasing S.

HTH,

--

messages.body_plain:
'Morning, Thomas !

Le vendredi 20 juin 2014 10:49:42 UTC+2, Thomas Moran a écrit :
> Hi Emmanuel, thanks for your remarks. I was perhaps not explicit enough that my change point Tcp is for the latent variable t (time), not x. That is, the functional response y = f(x) changes at some time t = Tcp.

Ah ! Okay. But you still don't have to estimate a[2] if your latent "time" has  no discontinuities.

>
> However, the more extensive model that I'm developing does involve change points for x as well, and I'll think about whether the continuous form you suggested could be used there.
>
>
>
> On Fri, Jun 20, 2014 at 12:59 AM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > A few remarks below :
> >
> > Le jeudi 19 juin 2014 04:50:04 UTC+2, Thomas Moran a écrit :
> > >
> > > Hi everyone,
> > >
> > > I’m here to ask for some guidance with design of a model that detects latent temporal change points in regression parameters. I’ve been dabbling with RStan for a few months and am really impressed with the documentation and support, but as a novice Bayesian I’ve run into a sticking point that, with any luck, will be trivial to someone more experienced.
> > >
> > > tl;dr - looking for Stan approach to infer step-change of regression parameters before and after a latent temporal change point.
> > >
> > > The simple case I’ll use for illustration is univariate linear regression of response variable y as a function of predictor x, which is a random variable drawn once per time step from a normal distribution N(.) . There is also a Gaussian noise term in the response, with standard deviation sig_y.
> > >
> > > y = a + b*x + noise —> y ~ N(a + b*x, sig_y)
> > >
> > > x ~ N(.)
> > >
> > > Could hardly be simpler. In the system under study, there is reason to believe that the system undergoes a step change in functional response, and thus regression parameters, at some change point time Tcp, such that:
> > >
> > > y ~ N(a[1] + b[1]*x, sig_y)   for t <= Tcp
> > >
> > > y ~ N(a[2] + b[2]*x, sig_y)  for t >   Tcp
> > >
> > > My objective is to infer Tcp, a[1:2], and b[1:2].
> > Ahem ! There is no a[2] to estimate : at x=Tcp, y=a[1]+b[1]*Tcp=a[2]+b[2]*Tcp ==> a[2]=a[1]+Tcp*(b[1]-b[2]).
> >
> > Introducing an unnecessary parameter may lead to serious convergence issues...
> >
> > >
> > > As posed, Tcp is discrete and thus can’t be directly represented in Stan. I implemented a hack solution in Stan that just pretends Tcp is continuous, which essentially treats any value of Tcp between time steps as equally likely. This actually works sometimes (meaning it converges and correctly estimates synthetic data parameters) but other times it fails badly (doesn’t converge, incorrect inference). I imagine this abuse of parameters has any number of undesirable consequences.
> > See above.
> > >
> > > I've attached the Stan code for this hack, as well as synthetic data (n=80, true parameters: Tcp=48, a[1] = 0, b[1] = 1, a[2] = 1, b[2] = 0.5, sig_y = 0.5) and the R code for generating random data.
> > >
> > > The manual and other discussions recommend “summing out” latent variables for mixing problems, but this isn’t really a mixing problem because the grouping is a deterministic function of Tcp, and anyway Tcp is the sought parameter. For this phase of my analysis I would be happy to estimate Tcp alone, and perhaps if I were more clever it would be obvious how to sum out the other parameters and end up with a continuous representation of the change point. But so far I’m not that clever.
> >
> > What would be wrong with a continuous time and modelling by y~a+log(e^(S*k1*(x_Tcp))/(1+e^(S*k2*(x-Tcp))))/S+\epsilon ? This is smooth, has slopes k1 for x<<Tcp, k1-k2 for x>>Tcp and the junction of the two segments becomes sharper with increasing S.
> >
> > HTH,
> >
> > --
> > Emmanuel Charpentier
> > >
> > > Many Thanks,
> > >
> > > -Thomas
> > >
> > >
> > > Note:
> > >
> > > My actual model is considerably more complicated, accounting for multiple error sources following the hierarchical approach described in
> > >
> > > Kelly, B. C. (2007), Some Aspects of Measurement Error in Linear Regression of Astronomical Data, Astrophys. J., 665(2), 1489, doi:10.1086/519947.
> > >
> > > and extended to a constrained segmented linear model that is applied to hydrologic data with threshold behavior. The approach works well for lumped data (no temporal change points), but the small successes I’ve had with estimating Tcp for the simplified example above entirely fail for the more complex model.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can Stan do mixed membership?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can Stan do mixed membership?
messages.body_plain:
I think I did a model like this in Stan a few months ago, so it's definitely possible. I say "I think", because the Bristol documentation style is very black-box, in my experience, so I don't know if what I did is what they mean by mixed/multiple membership.

The example I think of often is grant review committees, in which the decision for a grant proposal depends upon features of multiple raters. So predicting overall rating of a proposal requires accounting for features of each individual rater, combined through some (possibly non-additive) function. This seems like the case where outcome for a firm depends upon features of different nations it operates in.

The only trick I think is to set up a regular varying intercepts model, and then combine the varying intercepts to construct each prediction. Sounds like the firm example is just an additive combination with known weights, so should be possible to set up a weighted average of varying intercepts on nations in the linear predictor for the outcome.

Does this sound like the right interpretation?

That would indeed be straightforward to code in Stan.
And it should fit well.

> The example I think of often is grant review committees, in which the decision for a grant proposal depends upon features of multiple raters. So predicting overall rating of a proposal requires accounting for features of each individual rater, combined through some (possibly non-additive) function. This seems like the case where outcome for a firm depends upon features of different nations it operates in.

I don't see how this is related, but I've built lots of
these rating models over the past few years.
I formulated them a la Dawid and Skene (1979)
as measurement error models --- there's a latent true rating
and then each rater has a response based on the true rating
and perhaps other features of the item.  The responses can
be categorical, ordinal, or even continuous.  They've gotten
very popular with the ease of collecting crowdsourced data.
Marc Girolami and collaborators had a cool paper with GP priors
for ordinal data;  Uebersax and Grove had a neat latent continuous
ordinal model in the early 90s.

- Bob

Thanks everyone,

I think I managed to get the constraints working  for an KxD rectangular factor loading matrix, where D is the number of dimensions (i.e. factors).  Here is the code:

transformed parameters{
matrix[K,D]  alpha;
{
int index;

for (j in 1:D) {
    alpha[j,j] <- 1;
    for (i in (j+1):K) {
      index <- index + 1;
      alpha[i,j] <- offdiag[index];} // offdiag is a D*(K-D)+(D*(D-1)/2) vector specified a prior in the model block
}

for(i in 1:K){
     for(j in (i+1):D){
     alpha[i,j] <- 0;}
}

}
}

However, the constraints themselves don't seem to be sufficient to restrict the likelihood to a single mode, which somehow contradicts the literature. Also, why are the enclosing braces necessary to define" int index"? Without them, I get an error message "integer parameters or transformed parameters are not allowed.

Rick,

On Saturday, June 21, 2014 12:25:58 PM UTC-4, Rick Farouni wrote:
> However, the constraints themselves don't seem to be sufficient to restrict the likelihood to a single mode, which somehow contradicts the literature.

The reason there is not a single mode is that you can permute the factors and permute the loadings accordingly without changing the likelihood. Also, post-processing the output of Stan tends not to work well when there are multiple equivalent modes. You might be better off restricting the diagonal of the loadings matrix to be a copy of a positive_ordered variable and restrict the factor variances to be one.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
the two steps the paper i attached proposes to post-identify draws will work and the steps are easy to implement, so it's not hard to test.  the varimax step reduces general rotational invariance (which is uncountable) to a countable permutation invariance (with sign flips).  this is just a standard label switching problem and the second step in the paper resolves it.   this procedure will work with output from STAN, JAGS or any other solver.  the point is not the estimation algorithm (assuming the chains are converged), but the probability model definition.

mixing issues aside, the fundamental problem with using a lower triangular with positive diagonals restriction on the loadings matrix to fix a rotation is that this constraint induces a non-exchangeable prior on the communality - where founder factors receive a smaller prior variance than other loadings parameters.  the result (which is well known) is that the posterior is sensitive - varies with the ordering of variables, unlike EFA under MLE.  so it's really a good idea to dispense with the restriction.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Exploratory Factor Analysis and the Cholesky Factor
messages.body_plain:
For multiple modes --- regardless of whether they are exactly equivalent --- HMC will have difficulty because the Hamiltonian proposal tends to be toward the closest mode, but that is true for a lot of MCMC algorithms. The adaptation of NUTS is further jeopardized for a variety of reasons including that it is assuming constant curvature, which wouldn't be the case under multimodality. Furthermore, if the posterior distribution has a long ridge, it might keep leapfrogging indefinitely along that ridge. Basically, it is not real good at all in situations like this. There is more somewhere in the manual in the subsection about difficult posteriors.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Fit Parameters of Bivariate Normal Probability
messages.subject_clean: Fit Parameters of Bivariate Normal Probability
messages.body_plain:
What are you exactly trying to do? My first intuition would be that in the model block, you should evaluate x (the random variable) rather than y (a density). Keep in mind that "sampling" statements in the model block (e.g. x ~ multi_normal(mu,sigma) simply represent adding the log-probability/density of (x | mu,sigma) to the log-posterior (leaving out any constants).

Why do you need the density y?

Also, if you want to extend the dimensions of this model, I recommend you take a look at some of the native parameter types that could make your life a lot easier (correlation matrices and cholesky factors, starting with the first). The simple constraints on rho that you have now will only work in the two-dimensional case; for higher dimensions, this approach will not guarantee that the covariance matrix is positive-definitive and will lead to a lot of Metropolis rejections and inefficient sampling. Cholesky factors have the added benefit of cranking down the computational effort through (no inversion of the full covariance matrix required).

Luc

messages.body_plain:
I think the main problem here is that it is inappropriate to use an iid standard normal prior on a positive_ordered variable. That said, we don't have any good suggestions for such a prior. So, probably in this case, it would be better to make the diagonal elements positive but not necessarily ordered and put some appropriate prior on them.

You can speed up your code a little bit by making F a matrix and y a concatenated vector, in which case the guts of the model could be written as

  offdiag ~ normal(0,sigma_L);
  diag ~ something;
  sigma_L ~ cauchy(0,5);
  to_vector(F) ~ normal(0,1);
  y ~ normal(to_vector(F * L'), 1);

That still converges slowly with all the factor scores. So, for a pure EFA model the way psychologists estimate it, I would specify it in terms of the manifest covariance matrix having a Wishart likelihood.

messages.body_plain:
On Jun 23, 2014, at 6:13 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I think the main problem here is that it is inappropriate to use an iid standard normal prior on a positive_ordered variable.

Inappropriate how?

I just made a note to drop in some advice in the next
version of the manual, but I'm not sure what to tell people.

If you give an ordered vector variable components an i.i.d. normal,
then I believe the result is the same as if you'd provided
the same prior for an unconstrained vector and then sorted.

Another alternative would be to put a prior on the first
element and then on the differences (probably two different
priors, and the prior is probably different for positive_ordered
and ordered).

I remember asking Andrew what he'd prefer here without getting
an answer.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The extract() function scrambles the draws by design.
Here's the relevant doc line:

  extract(object, pars, permuted = TRUE, inc_warmup = FALSE)

If you want the same results, you need

  permuted=FALSE

We debated this behavior long and hard, and I have to
admit I lost the battle.   I would not have had permutation
as the default, but Andrew thought it was important so that
users didn't make mistakes like taking the first 500 draws
of four chains --- the default prevents that.

Now I think you can set the PRNG seed in R so that you
get the same behavior each time, but I'm not 100% sure.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Jun 23, 2014, at 7:15 PM, Sam Weiss <samc...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi again. I'm running the code below (same data) but its taking over 24 hours to complete... I'd like to do this with more than 2 time series as well. Is the code misspecified or inefficiently writen?
>
> Thanks,
>
>
> library(rstan)
> set_cppo("fast")
>
>
> code1=
>   "data {
> int<lower=0> N;
> int<lower=1> K;
> vector[K] y[N];
>
> }
> parameters {
> corr_matrix[K] OmegaV;
> vector<lower=0>[K] tauV;
> corr_matrix[K] OmegaW;
> vector<lower=0>[K] tauW;
> vector[K] theta[N];
>
> }
> transformed parameters{
> matrix[K,K] SigmaV;
> matrix[K,K] SigmaW;
> cov_matrix[2] Sigmavprior;
>
>
> SigmaV <- diag_matrix(tauV) * OmegaV * diag_matrix(tauV);
>
> SigmaW <- diag_matrix(tauW) * OmegaW * diag_matrix(tauW);

There are more efficient scaling operations.  diag_pre_multiply()
and diag_post_multiply() in Stan 2.2.  In Stan 2.3 (out any
minute, really), there will also be a direct quadratic form that
will do this all at once.

>
>
> Sigmavprior[1,1] <- 100;
> Sigmavprior[2,2]<- 100;
> Sigmavprior[1,2] <- 0;
> Sigmavprior[2,1] <- 0;
>
> }

If you have anything constant like Sigmavprior, it's much
more efficient to define it as transformed data.  All variables
should basically be declared in the earliest block that's feasible.

Also, no point making a diagonal covariance matrix.  You can just
sample the components independently with a vectorized univariate
normal, replacing

> theta[1]~multi_normal(y[1], Sigmavprior);

with

  theta[1] ~ multi_normal(y[1],100);

Now having said all this, you probably want to work directly
with Cholesky factors.  You can do this one of two ways.  Either
declare the Cholesky factors as variables (more efficient), or
Cholesky factorize a covariance matrix in the model itself and reuse
it with multi_normal_cholesky().  Alas, the Cholesky factor for
covariance matrix type is broken due to a misspelled error check in
2.2 (Ben --- this is why we try to be thorough in our signature
tests --- this one obviously didn't have enough testing);  that's fixed
in 2.3 and there's also a Cholesky factor for correlation matrices type
and some explicit advice on how to use it in the manual.

> model{
> //prior
> theta[1]~multi_normal(y[1], Sigmavprior);
> //likelihood
> for(n in 2:N){
> theta[n]~multi_normal(theta[n-1],SigmaW);
> y[n]~multi_normal(theta[n],SigmaV);
>
> }
>

The implicit prior on covariances is improper, which can slow
down sampling --- are you seeing big excursions?

I like the first line written the other way around as
the equivalent

  y[1] ~ multi_normal(theta[1], Sigmavprior);

to make it clear it's really part of the likelihood and to
make it clear you don't really have a prior here for theta[1].
Then you can add

  theta[1] ~ normal(0,100);

if you want, but that prior's probably so weak as to have almost
no effect if your data are on a standardized scale.

- Bob
