messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Exploratory Factor Analysis and the Cholesky Factor
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, June 23, 2014 1:05:40 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>
> On Jun 23, 2014, at 6:13 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> > I think the main problem here is that it is inappropriate to use an iid standard normal prior on a positive_ordered variable.
>
> Inappropriate how?

The elements are not independent due to the ordering, so iid anything is not great. Furthermore, the normal distribution isn't appropriate because each element is bounded on one or both sides, and the normalization factor is a function of the adjacent random variables. And in this case, having a prior mean zero for a positive random variable probably puts too much mass at zero when those diagonal elements need to be bounded away from zero for likelihood-identification.

Ben

Hi,

What I am trying to do is explore the influence of priors on the analysis of study results. Specifically this is what I wanted to examine wrt medical studies:
1) RCT, less biased for treatment effects, possibly underestimate adverse events
2) Observational studies, biased for treatment effects, better estimate of adverse events

So I wanted to use different priors in situations 1 and 2:
1) RCT:
- empirical bayesian prior (with goal of being mildly informative to give more weight to study data) for mean
- default uninformative prior for variance
2) Observational:
- default uninformative prior for mean
- empirical bayesian mildly informative prior for variance

I was hoping for some guidelines on how to achieve these different priors?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Empirical Bayes?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Empirical Bayes?
messages.body_plain:
> OK, I probably don't understand the concept of empirical bayes priors well.
>
> What I want is to have more informative priors that give more weight to the data in certain circumstance for both the mean and variance. Is there any "default" way to do this?

Not in the way you’re describing.

Empirical Bayes tries to use the data twice — once to define the prior and once to define the likelihood.  This
leads to overfitting and poor estimation in complicated models.

But Empirical Bayes is just an estimate of the full hierarchical model to which Andrew was referring.  In fact
you can think about Empirical Bayes as building a full hierarchical model and then making point estimates of
the hyper parameters.  The point estimates lead to underestimated uncertainty… just as we would expect
from overfitting.

To summarize, Empirical Bayes is an approximation of a full hierarchical model.  Any kind of “automated” or
“default” approach would require building the full model, with all those hyper priors, and then making point
estimates of the hyper parameters with something like maximum marginal likelihood, which has not yet
been implemented in Stan.

messages.subject: Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
messages.subject_clean: Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
messages.body_plain:
Hello fellow stan users,

I’m writing to solicit suggestions for improving the speed of sampling from my model.

I am interested in fitting the following model

y ~ Poisson(theta_j*q_j)

where theta_j is a positive number and q_j is a probability, indexed by j groups of observations. The goal of this project to (eventually) estimate both theta_j and q_j as linear functions of predictors under transformation, but at the moment I am struggling with the simpler task of efficiently estimating the constant term for each. (In my notation, theta=exp(X*beta) and logit(q)=Z*gamma, where X and Z are matrices of covariates and beta and gamma are vectors of coefficients, but this is only relevant to the future task of estimating coefficient terms.)

Clearly, one source of difficulty for this model is that it is not identified because there are infinitely many pairs theta, q which have the same product. Taking the tips from “Problematic Posteriors” section of the stan modeling reference, I’ve attempted to identify this model via prior specification. I believe that the model is sufficiently identified that it must be proper (though perhaps I have missed a subtlety which is preventing efficient runtime).

Simulated data for j=4 achieved R_hat <1.1 in 1500 iterations, taking between 570 and 670 seconds total per chain; however, n_eff is in the dozens for some parameter estimates. However, posterior medians are reasonably near the true values of the parameters for a synthetic data created with known, fixed theta and q, so I believe that the model is identified.

In simulated data, a plot of theta, q pairs clearly fall in a “sharply bent cigar” pattern. I believe that this might be the source of the problem: while stan is able to identify the “ridge” for which the product theta*q is plausible for a given y, it is difficult to sample from within that shape, likely since its contours are so stark. If the sampler steps in the wrong direction, it falls into the abyss. This implies a re-parameterization might be in order.

I’ve advanced my line of thinking this far: since we know mean(y) is the MLE for the Poisson distribution, deriving this quantity for each sector might go quite far in eliminating some wasteful rejections or wanderings, since “discovering” mean(y) reveals the best “ridge” along which sampling should be conducted. This implies that we want to conduct sampling along the line ln(mean(y))=ln(theta)+ln(q) that falls in the vicinity of the prior. But this is as far as I’ve gotten. Additionally, I’m concerned that this “trick” might not generalize well in the case when I’m trying to fit more than just an intercept: figuring out how to sample in a space near ln(mean(y))=X*beta-log(1+exp(-Z*gamma)) seems difficult, but perhaps I simply lack imagination.

V/r,

David Elkind

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Model design: detect latent temporal change points in regression parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Model design: detect latent temporal change points in regression parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Following Emmanuel’s lead, I found it simpler to use a smooth
analytical approximation of a step function to model the latent change
point. For the simple case of a linear regression y(x,t) with
intercept at 0 and change in slope only, the model can be stated as:

y = (b + db * H(t) )*x + noise

where b is slope, db is the change in slope, and

H(t) = 1/( 1 + exp( -(t - Tcp)*A) )

is a logistic function approximation to the Heaviside function with
that is ~0 for t < Tcp and ~1 for t > Tcp, with transition shape
parameter A.

The implementation in Stan:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;   // data count
  vector[N] x;        // predictor (covariate)
  vector[N] y;        // outcome (variate)
  vector[N] t;         // time
}
parameters {
  real b;                                 // slope
  real db;                               // slope change
  real<lower=0> sigma;           // noise
  real<lower=1,upper=N> Tcp; // change point time
}
model {
  vector[N] mu_y;                   // modeled y
  real H;                                 // smooth logistic
approximation to Heaviside function
  for (n in 1:N){
    H <- 1/(1+exp(-(t[n]-Tcp)*10));     // sampling sensitive to
exponent coefficient
    mu_y[n] <- (b + db*H)*x[n];         // modeled y
  }
  y ~ normal(mu_y,sigma);              // observed y with noise
}

An example data file is attached, and Stan recovers the true values b
= 1, db = -0.5, sigma = 0.5, Tcp = 48, with seemingly good
convergence.

So, am I missing any gotchas or pitfalls with this approach?

Incidentally, I made a couple attempts at marginalizing the latent
variable t, but besides the inefficiency that Bob mentioned I also
found it to be conceptually more difficult than the analytic approach
described above. I wonder if could convince someone (perhaps Luc?) to
apply this type of marginalization of a latent discrete change point
to the Stan manual mixture model as an example case?

Cheers,
-Thomas

>>>>

>>>>

>>>>

>>>>

>>>

>>> y=a[1]+b[1]*Tcp=a[2]+b[2]*Tcp ==> a[2]=a[1]+Tcp*(b[1]-b[2]).
>>>
>>> Introducing an unnecessary parameter may lead to serious convergence
>>> issues...
>>>
>>>>
>>>> As posed, Tcp is discrete and thus can’t be directly represented in
>>>> Stan. I implemented a hack solution in Stan that just pretends Tcp is
>>>> continuous, which essentially treats any value of Tcp between time steps as
>>>> equally likely. This actually works sometimes (meaning it converges and
>>>> correctly estimates synthetic data parameters) but other times it fails
>>>> badly (doesn’t converge, incorrect inference). I imagine this abuse of
>>>> parameters has any number of undesirable consequences.
>>>

>>>>

>>>> (n=80, true parameters: Tcp=48, a[1] = 0, b[1] = 1, a[2] = 1, b[2] = 0.5,
>>>> sig_y = 0.5) and the R code for generating random data.
>>>>
>>>> The manual and other discussions recommend “summing out” latent
>>>> variables for mixing problems, but this isn’t really a mixing problem
>>>> because the grouping is a deterministic function of Tcp, and anyway Tcp is
>>>> the sought parameter. For this phase of my analysis I would be happy to

>>> y~a+log(e^(S*k1*(x_Tcp))/(1+e^(S*k2*(x-Tcp))))/S+\epsilon ? This is smooth,

>>>
>>> HTH,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Power and absolute function
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Power and absolute function
messages.body_plain:
As you note, they are not currently vectorized.

Vectorizing either of these is not going to add
to the speed, which is from taking derivatives.

I doubt evaluating these functions is what is slow.

We do plan to vectorize more and more of our basic functions
as we go.  But it's not an immediate priority.

fabs() can cause a problem with sampling in HMC in that it
introduces a non-differentiable point at 0 and potentially
multiple modes.  There are usually better alternatives to using
fabs() directly, such as declaring variables in such a way as
to maintain positivity or using exp() if you just need to make
something positive.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Fitting an Poisson regression that is not identified
messages.body_plain:
A problem that can arise in very weakly identified models, by
which I mean ones where the posterior mean or median is
technically identified, but the posterior is relatively flat
around the mean.  There's a discussion in the manual in the
problematic posteriors chapter.

The usual solution is to tighten priors.  This can almost always
be done with very little affect on the solutions --- that is,
going from a very vague prior to one that's weakly informative.
For example normal(0,5) for a logistic regression coefficient compared
to normal(0,100) will make a big difference in computation without
affecting the posterior distribution much at all (assuming the predictor's
standardized and the data's not separable or close to it), especially in
cases where there's not much data.

Weak hyperpriors can cause the same kind of problem, with broad
swaths of the posterior having similar density, requiring a lot
of work to explore for the sampler.

More specifics below.

On Jun 23, 2014, at 11:59 PM, dje <djel...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello fellow stan users,
>
> I’m writing to solicit suggestions for improving the speed of sampling from my model.
>
> I am interested in fitting the following model
>
> y ~ Poisson(theta_j*q_j)
>
> where theta_j is a positive number and q_j is a probability, indexed by j groups of observations. The goal of this project to (eventually) estimate both theta_j and q_j as linear functions of predictors under transformation, but at the moment I am struggling with the simpler task of efficiently estimating the constant term for each. (In my notation, theta=exp(X*beta) and logit(q)=Z*gamma, where X and Z are matrices of covariates and beta and gamma are vectors of coefficients, but this is only relevant to the future task of estimating coefficient terms.)

Depending on values, it might be more stable to work on the log scale.

 y ~ poisson_log(X*beta + log_inv_logit(Z * gamma));

where we have

 poisson_log(y|alpha) = poisson(y|exp(alpha))

>
> Clearly, one source of difficulty for this model is that it is not identified because there are infinitely many pairs theta, q which have the same product. Taking the tips from “Problematic Posteriors” section of the stan modeling reference, I’ve attempted to identify this model via prior specification. I believe that the model is sufficiently identified that it must be proper (though perhaps I have missed a subtlety which is preventing efficient runtime).
>
> Simulated data for j=4 achieved R_hat <1.1 in 1500 iterations, taking between 570 and 670 seconds total per chain; however, n_eff is in the dozens for some parameter estimates. However, posterior medians are reasonably near the true values of the parameters for a synthetic data created with known, fixed theta and q, so I believe that the model is identified.

You may find with more data that you get a better behaved
posterior.

>
> In simulated data, a plot of theta, q pairs clearly fall in a “sharply bent cigar” pattern. I believe that this might be the source of the problem: while stan is able to identify the “ridge” for which the product theta*q is plausible for a given y, it is difficult to sample from within that shape, likely since its contours are so stark. If the sampler steps in the wrong direction, it falls into the abyss. This implies a re-parameterization might be in order.

Reparameterization can often help.  The problem with
banana-like densities is that their curvature varies
over their support, making it impossible to properly
adapt Euclidean HMC as used in Stan.  The result is that
you have to use smaller step sizes to get accurate
results (in practice, set the acceptance target higher to
make sure you're getting stable results).

> I’ve advanced my line of thinking this far:

Plotting the posterior to see what's going on is most of the battle!

> since we know mean(y) is the MLE for the Poisson distribution, deriving this quantity for each sector might go quite far in eliminating some wasteful rejections or wanderings, since “discovering” mean(y) reveals the best “ridge” along which sampling should be conducted. This implies that we want to conduct sampling along the line ln(mean(y))=ln(theta)+ln(q) that falls in the vicinity of the prior. But this is as far as I’ve gotten. Additionally, I’m concerned that this “trick” might not generalize well in the case when I’m trying to fit more than just an intercept: figuring out how to sample in a space near ln(mean(y))=X*beta-log(1+exp(-Z*gamma)) seems difficult, but perhaps I simply lack imagination.

In my experience, adding an intercept can often help immensely
in these models if you don't already have a column of 1 values
in X to act as an intercept.

Keep in mind that everything samples on the unconstrained parameters in Stan,
and that's where you want to look for nice covexity and peakiness
properties.

Others are better at this kind of thing than me.
If you create another post that just has a tight model definition
and asks about reparameterizations, Andrew or Michael or Ben can
probably help out.

- Bob

messages.subject: How to simulate quantities of interest using arm or rstanarm packages?
messages.subject_clean: How to simulate quantities of interest using arm or rstanarm packages?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Very newbie question here. I would like to know how to simulate quantities of interest out of a regression model estimated using either the arm or the rstanarm packages in R. I am just starting to use Bayesian methods and R and have been using the Zelig package for some time. I asked a similar question before <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/21057548/how-can-one-simulate-quantities-of-interest-from-the-posterior-density-in-mcmcgl>, but I would like to know if it is possible to simulate those quantities using the posterior distribution estimated by those packages.

In Zelig you can set the values you want for the independent values and it calculates the results for the outcome variable (expected value, probability, etc). An example:
# Creating a dataset:
x <- rnorm(100,20,10)
z <- rnorm(100,10,5)
e <- rnorm(100,0,1)
y <- 2*x+3*z+e
df <- data.frame(x,z,e,y)

# Loading Zelig
require(Zelig)

# Model
m1.zelig <- zelig(y ~ x + z, model="ls", data=df)
summary(m1.zelig)

# Simulating z = 10
s1 <- setx(m1.zelig, z = 10)
simulation <- sim(m1.zelig, x = s1)
summary(simulation)

So Zelig keeps x at its mean (20.56), and simulates the quantity of interest with z = 10. In this case, y is approximately 71.

The same model using arm:
# Model
require(arm)
m1.arm <- bayesglm(y ~ x + z, data=df)
summary(m1.arm)

And using rstanarm:
# Model
require(rstanarm)
m1.stan <- stanlm(y ~ x + z, data=df)
print(m1.stan)

Is there any way to simulate z = 10 and x equals to its mean with the posterior distribution estimated by those two packages and get the expected value of y?

Thank you very much for your attention,

Danilo

messages.subject_clean: How to simulate quantities of interest using arm or rstanarm packages?
messages.body_plain:
Like Bob said, you can do things like this in the generated quantities block of a .stan file (the ones in rstanarm are hardcoded without generated quantities in addition to being unfinished).

To do it in R, you need to do setx() yourself, but the posterior simulations of the parameters can be obtained in various ways. Probably the route that is most similar to Zelig would be

stanfit <- stan(...)
posterior <- as.matrix(stanfit)

You could then matrix multiply the x vector by (some subset of the columns of) posterior and then go on to construct your quantities of interest.

For arm, there is also a sim() function which draws parameters from the estimated sampling distribution.

Ben

It's not iterations, but time to convergence and then time
per effective sample after that that matters.

Stan's not just a graphical modeling language --- you can
write down any expression that's equal to the log posterior
up to an additive constant.

models that have continuous parameters in Stan.  We've fit
all kinds of models that people have written complicated

explore posteriors that vary dramatically in density.  Michael's
written about it pretty extensively in his papers and I think

falling "down" toward the mode, not climbing "up" a hill.

messages.body_plain:
The goal of enumerating beta0 and gamma0 in this way is to allow for a hierarchical structure to the model, so that beta0[j] refers to the jth grouping (sector) of observations. *_mu is the mean of these group-level effects, while *_eta and *_tau allow the direction and magnitude of the effect to vary for each sector, while still restricting it to be somewhere near *_mu.

This explanation is not mutually exclusive with your proposal being correct, though. Perhaps it is simply expensive to simultaneously identify both theta and q AND the hierarchical structure at the same time. I had hoped that the hierarchical structure would help enforce some regularity across sectors, thereby making it easier to estimate theta and q, but the cost is, of course, introducing additional free parameters, so perhaps it's a wash.

> I think that there is actually two levels of "non identification" in the current model. The first one is, as you say, that there is infinitely many pairs of theta and q. But the second one is due that q and theta are modelled as a linear function of other parameters (no data involved), ie:

>     beta0  <- beta0_mu+beta0_tau*beta0_eta;
>     gamma0 <- gamma0_mu+gamma0_tau*gamma0_eta;
>

In the final model, if I understood correctly, beta0_eta and gamma0_eta would be data, right? That would be better, as it eliminates this problem.

Thanks for the thoughts. I've had some (apparent) success with the
smooth ridge approach, which the astute Stan user will recognize as
the built-in inv_logit() function. That is, multiple chains with
different starting values converge to the same, accurate estimate.

drastically with transition slope. My heuristic solution to this has
been to keep the slope as shallow as possible, i.e. set the shape
parameter so that the ridge transition span is comparable to the data
interval. So far, so good, but I'll need to check out Bob's suggested
reading to convince myself I really understand what's going on.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

Like Bob said (and I should have realized this as well), all chains will converge to the same mode as the ridges do not prohibit this. However, HMC will probably oversample the area directly around the mode, and undersample values further away from the mode. I.e. the uncertainty of the parameter estimates (not just that of the latent temporal point) will be underestimated. There is no guarantee that decreasing the slope of your logistic function allows appropriate sampling of all regions of the posterior. One more vote for a mixture model :).

Luc

messages.body_plain:
Multimodality is rarely the answer and almost always indicates a poorly designed model.  In particular, a multimodal model makes sense only if you want to average over all the modes — if you want to condition on a single model and look at averages in that neighborhood then your model is inconsistent.

If we had an exact integrator then HMC would sample the mode and the tails exactly as necessary (technical note — perhaps not with geometric ergodicity but at the very least with uniform ergodicity).  In practice where we use a numerical integrator the finite step size may cause problems but these are readily diagnosed.  See, for example, http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906.  This is exactly what we would see if the ridge were to become very tight but by decreasing the step size appropriately the sampler would be able to explore everything (modulo a few technical details).

In any case, just make the slope a hyperparameter and give it a Gaussian hyperprior around where you are currently setting it by hand.  If the posterior for the slope is in tension with the prior then you know that there is trouble with the smooth turn on and can reevaluate your model.

messages.body_plain:
Mixture models have their own multimodality, where
the different modes are the same thing with labels
swapped.  You get the same kind of behavior in IRT
models with sign switching of alpha, beta, and delta

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(delta * (alpha - beta));

One approach is to sample around a single mode --- it's easy
enough to do in BUGS or Stan.  The mass doesn't normalize,
but that's not an issue.  What does seem like an issue is that
the shape of the density is wrong --- it'll have a trough
and then start heading up toward the other mode, whereas a
proper model's probability should continue to decline.
Now whether there's enough mass in that region to make a
difference is another matter --- if there were, the sampler
will bounce around modes and you have bigger problems.

So my question is how do we deal with this?  In IRT models,
we usually just constrain delta > 0, which gets rid of
the multimodality.  Is that always the right thing to do?
What's the equivalent for a mixture model?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> So my question is how do we deal with this?  In IRT models,
> we usually just constrain delta > 0, which gets rid of
> the multimodality.  Is that always the right thing to do?
> What's the equivalent for a mixture model?

That depends on the model.

The point is that the permutation invariance you see in mixture models has no meaning -- it's
just a consequence of having too many degrees of freedom.  Consequently the "right" answer
would be to find the correct minimal degrees of freedom but that doesn't exactly give a general
algorithm so it falls more into the domain of the folk theorem.

Multimodal models are hard to fit, but that's usually because you're not fitting the model you're
actually after.

messages.body_plain:
I think this deserves a blog post!  Here's a rough draft.

Robert grant writes,

> ... I feel that journal readers are poorly served by pages of algebra and no straightforward BUGS/Stan code. With good checking, it should be ok to present a new model in this way. After all, I don't have to write down the likelihood and Newton-Raphson every time I publish
> a logistic regression.

I (Bob) am always struck by this same issue.  Here's what I
think is going on:

1.  What goes in a paper is up to the author.  If the author
struggled with a step or found it a bit tricky to think
about themselves, then the struggle goes into the paper.  Even
if it might be obvious to someone with more experience in
a field.  I was just reading a paper with a very detailed
exposition of EM for a latent logistic regression problem with
conditional probability derivations, etc. (JMLR paper on
crowdsourcing by Raykar et al., which by the way is an awesome
paper, even if it suffers from this flaw and number 3.)

2.  What goes in a paper is up to editors.  If the editors
don't understand something, they'll ask for details, even
if they should be obvious to the entire field.  I find this
in applied papers in natural language processing, where
almost every paper that uses a notion like entropy (including
one I just wrote) redefines it from scratch.  Every bit
of algebra gets worked out because the audience isn't used
to working equations for themselves.  You have to insert p-values
even if you don't believe them.  You have to justify Bayesian inference
by comparing it to some frequentist alternative.  Etc., etc.
(Mitzi says whenever more than one academic gets togeter, the
topic eventually devolves to refereeing.  Maybe it's just me.)

3.  Authors tend to narratives over crisp expositions.  They want
to tell you their story of how they got to the conclusions.  (Even me,
hence the preface of the Stan manual.)  One of the things that frustrates me
to no end in papers, particularly in statistics, is that the author tells you
a narrative of how they meandered to the model they finally use; in computer
science, they meander in the same way to models or algorithm
variants.  What I want to see is a crisp statement of the model
with enough details that I can replicate it.  Providing working code is the
easiest way to do that.  It's why I liked Jennifer and Andrew's regression
book so much --- they gave you (mostly) runnable code.

I think what applied papers need to do is lay out their model crisply.
BUGS is a nice language for this if your model is easily expressed as a directed
acyclic graph.  I think the variable declarations in Stan make it even clearer
what's going on, especially as models go beyond a few lines.  The problem
with Stan, as Andrew and I were just discussing yesterday, is that you
have to lay out what is data and what is parameters (i.e., what you observe
and what you infer conditioned on those observations).

Mathematicians seem to be immune to problems (1) and (3).  In fact, I
feel they often go too far, which is why this is such a Goldilocks issue.
What's an inscrutable step or bit of math to one person (contact manifolds
anyone?) is like a logistic regression to another person.  You can't write
an intro to differentiable manifolds into every one of your papers.

- Bob

posterior if they were not well separated.

messages.body_plain:
In version 2.2.0, there are online gamma-related sampling statements "gamma" and "inv_gamma". I'm guessing it's the same in 2.3.0.

It seems you are trying to use the complementary cumulative distribution function for the gamma distribution as a probability density function. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gamma_ccdf compile error in 2.3.0, but only when using ~, not when using increment_log_prob
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gamma_ccdf compile error in 2.3.0, but only when using ~, not when using increment_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
gamma_ccdf() is a complementary cumulative distribution so
it wasn't intended be used with sampling notation (~) as a density.
What should happen is the parser should throw an error saying you
can't use gamma_ccdf as a density.

The reason you're getting what you're getting is that
the suffix "_log" is what we use to mark densities.  In retrospect,
that was a very bad decision --- we'll probably fix it in the near
future, but it's a lot of code renaming.  Here's the issue to
track the fix:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/711

- Bob

P.S.  We've been waiting for PyStan for the 2.3 announcement.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.body_plain:
Oops --- this one got hung up in my drafts.

I think the sphere is the first step to understanding
more general manifold cases.  So it'd be natural to do
spheres and then a more general Riemannian manifold case.

Simon Byrne gave a nice talk at MCMski about HMC on a sphere
with geodesics (great circles in the spherical case).

I don't think the spheres are too tricky for either Goodman
and Weare's walker moves or differential evolution updates.

I'm sure Michael could knock out the general definitions
for these ensemble methods if he were so inclined.

For the Goodman and Weare case, the volume adjustment for
Metropolis is going to be tricky (you move along a line there
and need to look at masses of neighborhoods on either end).

For differential evolution, I think you're going to need something
like parallel transport (as seen in Michael's generalization of NUTS)
in order to apply a line of movement between two randomly selected points
to a third point.

- Bob

>
> Spherical coordinates are going to be tricky because they have a different topology
> than what Stan can naively handle (S^{n - 1} vs R^{n}).  I’m not sure there’s a great
> answer yet — although there had previously been some thoughts on how to make
> it work with the addition of some clever priors.

> On Jun 19, 2014, at 6:28 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Hi Mike,
>>
>> I think the answer you are looking for is in the Stan manual, section "Automatic Relevance Detection" (p.147 of the Stan 2.2.0 manual). It basically boils down to allowing rho to vary by dimension. In your case, the two values of rho pertaining to space would be the same, and the third value of rho pertaining to time would be allowed to be estimated separately. Your suggestion of using two additive GPs would mean you would also allow eta to vary between time and space. I'm not sure whether this is necessary; it would add an extra parameter to the model that you might not need.
>>
>> Best,
>>
>> Luc
>>
>> On Thursday, 19 June 2014 08:26:29 UTC-7, Mike Lawrence wrote:
>> Hi folks,
>>
>> I'm finally getting to grips with GPs, and am now looking at the
>> multivariate case for application to my real-world data. Specifically,
>> I deal with EEG data where we get measure voltage as a function of
>> time and position on the skull. Taking a simple spherical model of the
>> skull, we can encode position in terms of longitude and latitude (or
>> phi & theta if you want to use polar coordinates). I see from the
>> example in the manual how to combine two variables where simple
>> euclidean distance is computed, i.e. (pg 144):
>>
>>      data {
>>        int<lower=1> D;
>>        int<lower=1> N;
>>        vector[D] x[N];
>>      }
>>      transformed data {
>>      ...
>>            Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-dot_self(x[i] - x[j]))
>>                          + if_else(i==j, 0.1, 0.0);
>>      ...
>>
>> Any ideas on how to do this with one simple continuous variate (time)
>> and spherical coordinates?
>>
>> Also, if I move to a fitting/inference context where I evaluate the GP
>> hyperparamters (eta, sigma, rho), presumably something should be done
>> to reflect the fact that time and spatial coordinates are very
>> different metrics and therefore might have different best-suited
>> hyperparameter values, no? The obvious solution would be to have two
>> additive GPs, one for time and one for the spherical coordinate, and
>> thus two sets of GP hyperparameters, but I don't want to assume that
>> the same temporal function exists at all spatial coordinates and vice
>> versa. Any thoughts?
>>
>> Thanks in advance,
>>
>> Mike
>>
>> --
>> Mike Lawrence
>> Graduate Student
>> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
>> Dalhousie University
>>
>> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

On 25 Jun 2014 11:47, "Michael Betancourt" <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Contact manifolds are the worst!
>
> I think that ultimately the issue is that people approach the unknown very differently.  The great scientists will understand they
> don't have the time to understand something, find what bits they might be able to understand, but don't stop others from
> exploring further.  Poor scientists will become defensive and prevent anyone from moving forward with methods/techniques
> that they don't understand.
>
> This frustrates publications, grants, algorithm adoption, and especially graduate advising.
>
> One great thing about the Stan modeling language is that it defines a vocabulary in which people can describe their model
> agnostic to the actual fitting methods.  That alone can go a long way to factoring the expertise needed to understand a paper.
>
>
> On Wed, Jun 25, 2014 at 10:37 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > I think this deserves a blog post!  Here's a rough draft.
> >
> > Robert grant writes,
> >
> > > ... I feel that journal readers are poorly served by pages of algebra and no straightforward BUGS/Stan code. With good checking, it should be ok to present a new model in this way. After all, I don't have to write down the likelihood and Newton-Raphson every time I publish
> > > a logistic regression.
> >
> > I (Bob) am always struck by this same issue.  Here's what I
> > think is going on:
> >
> > 1.  What goes in a paper is up to the author.  If the author
> > struggled with a step or found it a bit tricky to think
> > about themselves, then the struggle goes into the paper.  Even
> > if it might be obvious to someone with more experience in
> > a field.  I was just reading a paper with a very detailed
> > exposition of EM for a latent logistic regression problem with
> > conditional probability derivations, etc. (JMLR paper on
> > crowdsourcing by Raykar et al., which by the way is an awesome
> > paper, even if it suffers from this flaw and number 3.)
> >
> > 2.  What goes in a paper is up to editors.  If the editors
> > don't understand something, they'll ask for details, even
> > if they should be obvious to the entire field.  I find this
> > in applied papers in natural language processing, where
> > almost every paper that uses a notion like entropy (including
> > one I just wrote) redefines it from scratch.  Every bit
> > of algebra gets worked out because the audience isn't used
> > to working equations for themselves.  You have to insert p-values
> > even if you don't believe them.  You have to justify Bayesian inference
> > by comparing it to some frequentist alternative.  Etc., etc.
> > (Mitzi says whenever more than one academic gets togeter, the
> > topic eventually devolves to refereeing.  Maybe it's just me.)
> >
> > 3.  Authors tend to narratives over crisp expositions.  They want
> > to tell you their story of how they got to the conclusions.  (Even me,
> > hence the preface of the Stan manual.)  One of the things that frustrates me
> > to no end in papers, particularly in statistics, is that the author tells you
> > a narrative of how they meandered to the model they finally use; in computer
> > science, they meander in the same way to models or algorithm
> > variants.  What I want to see is a crisp statement of the model
> > with enough details that I can replicate it.  Providing working code is the
> > easiest way to do that.  It's why I liked Jennifer and Andrew's regression
> > book so much --- they gave you (mostly) runnable code.
> >
> > I think what applied papers need to do is lay out their model crisply.
> > BUGS is a nice language for this if your model is easily expressed as a directed
> > acyclic graph.  I think the variable declarations in Stan make it even clearer
> > what's going on, especially as models go beyond a few lines.  The problem
> > with Stan, as Andrew and I were just discussing yesterday, is that you
> > have to lay out what is data and what is parameters (i.e., what you observe
> > and what you infer conditioned on those observations).
> >
> > Mathematicians seem to be immune to problems (1) and (3).  In fact, I
> > feel they often go too far, which is why this is such a Goldilocks issue.
> > What's an inscrutable step or bit of math to one person (contact manifolds
> > anyone?) is like a logistic regression to another person.  You can't write
> > an intro to differentiable manifolds into every one of your papers.
> >

Sorry for the vague use of lassoing.By lassoing I meant that the model tries to find two non-trivial mixture components that are as far away from eachother as possible, but that also still explain the data, such that for each data points either of the following is as large as possible.
multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu1, Sigma1) - multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu2, Sigma2);  // Log-probability of occurring under MVN1, penalized propto 1 / P(occurring under MVN2)^lambda
multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu2, Sigma2) - multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu1, Sigma1);  // Log-probability of occurring under MVN2, penalized propto 1 / P(occurring under MVN1)^lambda

So maybe lasso is not really the best word here. Inverse lasso? In my previous code, the tuning parameter lambda is not specified and there assumed to be one (this goes beyond your question).

Apologies for the wild thoughts.

Luc

Let me try to remember what I did for differential evolution on hypersphere. If you have point A, B and C on surface of hypershere, and want to move from A to A + (B-C):

- reflect A in B to get A'
- reflect A' in C to get A''
- reflect A'' in A to get A'''
- split A and A'''

Simples!

Easy enough also to do A + a(B-C)

messages.subject: Stan 2.3 released (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan)
messages.subject_clean: Stan 2.3 released (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan)
messages.body_plain:
We're happy to announce RStan, PyStan and CmdStan 2.3.
Instructions on how to install at:

   http://mc-stan.org/

Release notes below.

As always, let us know if you're having problems or have comments
or suggestions.

- Stan Development Team

v.2.3.0 (18 June 2014)
======================================================================

We had a record number of user-submitted patches this go around.
Thanks to everyone!

New Features
------------
* user-defined function definitions added to Stan language
* cholesky_corr data type for Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
* a^b syntax for pow(a,b)  (thanks to Mitzi Morris)
* reshaping functions: to_matrix(), to_vector(), to_row_vector(),
  to_array_1d(), to_array_2d()
* matrix operations: quad_form_sym() (x' *Sigma * x), QR decompositions
  qr_Q(), qr_R()
* densities: Gaussian processes multi_gp_log(), multi_gp(),
  and alternative negative binomial parameterization neg_binomial_2()
* random number generator: multi_normal_cholesky_rng()
* sorting: sort_indices_*() for returning indexes in sorted order by
  value
* added JSON parser to C++ (not exposed through interfaces yet; thanks
  to Mitzi Morris)
* many fixes to I/O for data and inits to check consistency and
  report errors
* removed some uses of std::cout where they don't belong
* updated parser for C++11 compatibility (thanks to Rob Goedman)

New Developer
--------------
* added Marco Inacio as core developer

Optimizations
-------------
* turned off Eigen asserts
* efficiency improvements to posterior analysis print

Documentation
-------------
* Clarified licensing policy for individual code contributions
* Huge numbers of fixes to the documentation, including many
  user-contributed patches (thanks!), fixes to parallelization in
  CmdStan, Windows install instructions, boundaries for Dirichlet and
  Beta, removed suggestion to use floor and ceiling as indices,
  vectorized many models, clarified that && doesn't short circuit,
  clarified von Mises normalization, updated censoring doc (thanks
  to Alexey Stukalov), negative binomial doc enhanced, new references,
  new discussion of hierarchical models referencing Betancourt and
  Girolami paper,
* Avraham Aadler was particularly useful in pointing out and fixing
  documentation errors

Bug Fixes
------------
* fixed bug in lkj density
* fixed bug in Jacobian for corr_matrix data type
* fix cholesky_cov_matrix test code to allow use as parameter
* fixed poisson_rng, neg_binomial_rng
* allow binary operations (e.g., < and >) within range constraints
* support MS Visual Studio 2008
* fixed memory leaks in categorical sampling statement, categorical_log
  function, and softmax functions
* removed many compiler warnings
* numerous bug fixes to arithmetic test code conditions and messages,
  including calls from
* fixed model crashes when no parameter specified
* fixed template name conflicts for some compiler bugs (thanks Kevin
  S. Van Horn)

Code Reorganizations & Updates
------------------------------
* CmdStan is now in its own repository on GitHub: stan-dev/cmdstan
* consolidate and simplify error handling across modules
* pulled functionality from CmdStan command class and PyStan and RStan
  into Stan C++
* generalized some interfaces to allow std::vector as well as Eigen
  for compatibility
* generalize some I/O CSV writer capabilities
* optimization output text cleaned up
* integer overflow during I/O now raises informative error messages
* const correctness for chains (thanks Kevin S. Van Horn)

On Thu, Jun 26, 2014 at 8:47 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I would think you'd want to let the data induce the
> correct amount of separation in the means.
>
> For K-means, there's classically an issue with initialization.
> Strategies like K-means++ attempt to get good coverage in
> initialization by maximizing the distance between the
> initialized means.  But it's a chicken-and-egg problem, because
> if you knew where good centers were to start, you wouldn't need
> K-means in the first place.  K-means++ is neat in that it tries
> to balance coverage with distance apart, but it's still pretty
> crude.  More principled ways to do this are well beyond what
> I know how to do.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jun 26, 2014, at 4:43 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Sorry for the vague use of lassoing.By lassoing I meant that the model tries to find two non-trivial mixture components that are as far away from eachother as possible, but that also still explain the data, such that for each data points either of the following is as large as possible.

>>       * multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu1, Sigma1) - multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu2, Sigma2);  // Log-probability of occurring under MVN1, penalized propto 1 / P(occurring under MVN2)^lambda
>>       * multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu2, Sigma2) - multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu1, Sigma1);  // Log-probability of occurring under MVN2, penalized propto 1 / P(occurring under MVN1)^lambda

>> So maybe lasso is not really the best word here. Inverse lasso? In my previous code, the tuning parameter lambda is not specified and there assumed to be one (this goes beyond your question).
>>
>> Apologies for the wild thoughts.
>>
>> Luc
>>
>>
>> On Thursday, 26 June 2014 03:10:47 UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> You can assume the mixture probability is not
>> uniform and fit it.
>>
>> I'm not sure what you mean by lassoing.  Do you
>> want to eliminate dimensions from the clustering?
>> You can put hierarchical priors on the variances.
>> We can't technically do the L1 lasso because it's
>> not a Bayesian method.  Our optimization won't deal
>> with it either because it's gradient based and we
>> don't do anything special around 0 like truncation.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> On Jun 26, 2014, at 9:18 AM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> > I just realized that with that last piece of code (the bivariate normal distributions), I was trying to apply a clustering method without realizing it: generalized soft K-means! This method is also described in the Stan reference manual, p. 130 (v.2.2.0). Adapting the code from the manual to Thomas' problem leads to the code below. I think the major difference is that there is no lassoing in soft K-means as a priori data points are assumed to come from K different mixture components with equal probability. I would be happy to hear comments on the appropriateness of lassoing.
>> >
>> > data {
>> >   int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
>> >   int<lower=2> D; // number of dimensions
>> >   int<lower=2> K; // number of clusters
>> >   vector[D] Y[N];  // N sets of D-dimensional data points
>> > }
>> >
>> > transformed data {
>> >   real<upper=0> neg_log_K;
>> >   neg_log_K <- -log(K);
>> > }
>> >
>> > parameters {
>> >   ordered[K] mu_y;  // ordered location of mixture component along the last dimension
>> >   real mu_x[K,D-1];  // unordered location of mixture components along remaining dimensions
>> >   vector<lower=0> sigma[D];  // measurement error
>> >   corr_matrix[D] C[K];  // correlation matrices for mixture components
>> > }
>> >
>> > transformed parameters {
>> >   vector[D] Mu[K];  // location of mixture components
>> >   matrix[D,D] Sigma[K]; // covariance matrices for mixture component
>> >
>> >   for (k in 1:K) {
>> >     for (d in 1:(D-1)) {
>> >       Mu[k,d] <- mu_x[k,d]
>> >     }
>> >     Mu[k,D] <- mu_y[k]
>> >     Sigma[K] <- diag_pre_multply(sigma,C[K]);
>> >     Sigma[K] <- diag_post_multply(Sigma[K],sigma);
>> >   }
>> >
>> > }
>> >
>> > model {
>> >   vector[K] soft_z;
>> >
>> >   for (n in 1:N) {
>> >     for (k in 1:K) {
>> >       soft_z[k] <- neg_log_k - multi_normal_log(Y[n], Mu[k], Sigma[k]);
>> >     }
>> >     increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(soft_z));
>> >   }
>> > }
>> >
>> > generate quantities {
>> >   matrix[D-1,D-1] Sigma11[K];  // marginal covariance matrix for the first D-1 dimensions, which are intended as predictors
>> >   real Sigma22[K];  // marginal covariance of the last dimension, which is intended to be predicted
>> >   vector[D-1] Sigma21[K];  //  marginal covariance between first D-1 dimensions and the last dimension
>> >   vector[D-1] mu11[K];  // the means of the clusters on all but the last dimensions
>> >   real mu22[K];  // the means of the clusters on the last dimension
>> >   real sigma_cond[K]; // the standard error of the residuals on the last dimension, conditional on all other dimensions
>> >
>> >   vector[D-1] B0[K];  // cluster-specific intercepts for the regression line through the last dimension, conditional on all other dimensions
>> >   vector[D-1] B1[K];  // cluster-specific slopes for the regression line through the last dimension, conditional on all other dimensions
>> >
>> >   for (k in 1:K) {
>> >     mu22[k] <- mu[k,D];
>> >
>> >     for (d in 1:(D-1)) {
>> >       mu11[k,d] <- mu[k,d];
>> >       Sigma21[k,d] <- Sigma[k,d,1];
>> >
>> >       for (dd in 1:(D-1)) {
>> >         Sigma11[k,d,dd] <- Sigma[k,d,dd];
>> >       }
>> >
>> >     }
>> >     Sigma22[k] <- Sigma[k,D,D];
>> >
>> >     B1[k] <- Sigma12[k] / Sigma11[k];
>> >     B0[k] <- Mu22[k] - dot_product(B1[k], Mu11[k]);
>> >     sigma_cond[k] <- Sigma22[k] - B1[k] * Sigma21[k];
>> >   }
>> > }
>> >
>> > If anything crashes, I expect it to be the generated quantities. Apologies in advance :)!.
>> >

messages.subject: Re: Stan 2.3 released (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan)
messages.subject_clean: Stan 2.3 released (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan)
messages.body_plain:
My congratulations. I am really looking forward to start using these user-functions which will make my Stan code a lot better recyclable... and even force me write "nicer" Stan models...

... one note: If you write that a bug was fixed in lkj_density (or something with similar wide usage) I would appreciate if some note to its relevance could be given, i.e. is it minor or do I have to throw away my old inferences - just to be a bit extreme.

So maybe a link to the ticket or git commit or better a comment about the impact of the bug would be very user-friendly here. I know that Stan is already one of the most user-friendliest softwares out there, but as Stan is used for more and more "serious" stuff, a bug here and there could matter to some of us.

Many thanks for making the release again - looking forward to play with it!

Cheers,
Sebastian

On Thursday, June 26, 2014 6:50:46 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We're happy to announce RStan, PyStan and CmdStan 2.3.
> Instructions on how to install at:
>
>    http://mc-stan.org/
>
> Release notes below.
>
> As always, let us know if you're having problems or have comments
> or suggestions.
>
> - Stan Development Team
>
>
> v.2.3.0 (18 June 2014)
> ======================================================================
>
> We had a record number of user-submitted patches this go around.
> Thanks to everyone!
>
> New Features
> ------------
> * user-defined function definitions added to Stan language
> * cholesky_corr data type for Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
> * a^b syntax for pow(a,b)  (thanks to Mitzi Morris)
> * reshaping functions: to_matrix(), to_vector(), to_row_vector(),
>   to_array_1d(), to_array_2d()
> * matrix operations: quad_form_sym() (x' *Sigma * x), QR decompositions
>   qr_Q(), qr_R()
> * densities: Gaussian processes multi_gp_log(), multi_gp(),
>   and alternative negative binomial parameterization neg_binomial_2()
> * random number generator: multi_normal_cholesky_rng()
> * sorting: sort_indices_*() for returning indexes in sorted order by
>   value
> * added JSON parser to C++ (not exposed through interfaces yet; thanks
>   to Mitzi Morris)
> * many fixes to I/O for data and inits to check consistency and
>   report errors
> * removed some uses of std::cout where they don't belong
> * updated parser for C++11 compatibility (thanks to Rob Goedman)
>
> New Developer
> --------------
> * added Marco Inacio as core developer
>
> Optimizations
> -------------
> * turned off Eigen asserts
> * efficiency improvements to posterior analysis print
>
> Documentation
> -------------
> * Clarified licensing policy for individual code contributions
> * Huge numbers of fixes to the documentation, including many
>   user-contributed patches (thanks!), fixes to parallelization in
>   CmdStan, Windows install instructions, boundaries for Dirichlet and
>   Beta, removed suggestion to use floor and ceiling as indices,
>   vectorized many models, clarified that && doesn't short circuit,
>   clarified von Mises normalization, updated censoring doc (thanks
>   to Alexey Stukalov), negative binomial doc enhanced, new references,
>   new discussion of hierarchical models referencing Betancourt and
>   Girolami paper,
> * Avraham Aadler was particularly useful in pointing out and fixing
>   documentation errors
>
> Bug Fixes
> ------------
> * fixed bug in lkj density
> * fixed bug in Jacobian for corr_matrix data type
> * fix cholesky_cov_matrix test code to allow use as parameter
> * fixed poisson_rng, neg_binomial_rng
> * allow binary operations (e.g., < and >) within range constraints
> * support MS Visual Studio 2008
> * fixed memory leaks in categorical sampling statement, categorical_log
>   function, and softmax functions
> * removed many compiler warnings
> * numerous bug fixes to arithmetic test code conditions and messages,
>   including calls from
> * fixed model crashes when no parameter specified
> * fixed template name conflicts for some compiler bugs (thanks Kevin
>   S. Van Horn)
>
> Code Reorganizations & Updates
> ------------------------------
> * CmdStan is now in its own repository on GitHub: stan-dev/cmdstan
> * consolidate and simplify error handling across modules
> * pulled functionality from CmdStan command class and PyStan and RStan
>   into Stan C++
> * generalized some interfaces to allow std::vector as well as Eigen
>   for compatibility
> * generalize some I/O CSV writer capabilities
> * optimization output text cleaned up
> * integer overflow during I/O now raises informative error messages
> * const correctness for chains (thanks Kevin S. Van Horn)
>
>
>

messages.subject_clean: external functions in user-defined Stan functions?
messages.body_plain: I can't tell for sure from reading the manual whether or not one could use an external function in a user-defined Stan function. So, for example, it would be very useful if I could use a multivariate normal CDF function from the mnormt R package in a user-defined Stan function. It seems unlikely that just sticking an R (or Fortran, or whatever) function in there would work, but I want to confirm that this is the case.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob

Thanks for your reply. For some reason transposing (u[s] * gamma) also doesnt work. rstan still complains about it being a row vector.

Do you have any idea as to when request #608 will be fixed?

Thanks

Daniel

On Thursday, June 26, 2014 12:37:46 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Pull request #608, which fixes issue #589 is still held up
> in testing.  I'd thought it had already passed and been merged
> into 2.3.  It will allow vectors and row vectors to be used for
> the y in y ~ multi_normal(...); and will also allow vectorization in
> y (and I think mu).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Jun 25, 2014, at 11:01 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> >
> >

> > Hi Bob
> >
> > Sorry that I have to bother you with this again. I just updated to the new rstan version, however the error persists (see in red at the end of this post).
> >
> > The issue is with how you're calling multi_normal_log() and updating to a new rstan version isn't going to help.
> >
> >
> > I tried to transpose, as you suggested but that doesnt work either. I am not sure whether transforming beta (either by transposing or changing beta to an array of vectors) would change anything, as rstan seems to complain about the (u[s] * gamma) operation.
> >
> > You need to transpose the (u[s] * gamma) operation. The error message is telling you that the the second argument, (u[s] * gamma), is a row_vector. The available function signatures expects that to be a vector. In Stan, vector and row_vector are not equivalent.
> >
> >
> > Has the multi_normal issue not been fixed? What should I do?
> >
> > Is there an issue we're not aware of? The fix is to use the types correctly. That is, make sure the second argument is actually a vector, not a row vector. Can you try transposing the expression?
> >
> >
> >
> > Thanks
> >
> > Daniel

> >

> > > On Monday, June 9, 2014 11:59:28 AM UTC+1, Daniel Grigat wrote:

> > > I am trying to recreate the multivariate regression example from page 92 (section 9.9) in the most recent Rstan manual, as it fits the type of analysis that I want to run on a psychological experiment.
> > >
> > > My goal is to adjust the subject level data (‘groups’) that I have with the population/group-level predictors. Each subject undertakes 22 trials in a decision-making task, with binary responses. Hence I am using a linear regression model at the group level and a logistic function at the subject level.
> > >
> > > My problem is that I am running into a well-documented problem: I am creating a row-vector in line 27 when multiplying the group predictors (u[s]) with gamma. the multi-normal function only accepts vectors as inputs:
> > >
> > > Error in stanc("GBE_hierarchical_logistic_linear.stan") :
> > >
> > >   failed to parse Stan model 'GBE_hierarchical_logistic_linear' with error message:

> > > EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=27, column=56

> > >     arg 1 type=row vector

> > >     arg 2 type=matrix

> > > available function signatures for multi_normal_log:
> > >
> > > 0.  multi_normal_log(vector, vector, matrix) : real
> > >
> > > unknown distribution=multi_normal
> > >
> > > Parser expecting: <eps>
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > I simulated data to test this model. The simulated data is structured as follows: 50 subjects, three parameters to be estimated per subject, two group predictors, each subject's true parameters are drawn from a normal distribution, with non-zero mean and std. of 3.
> > >
> > > My questions:
> > >
> > > 1. Since I have exactly recreated the example rstan code given on page 95; I wonder whether I made a mistake or whether the example as described in the manual cannot currently be run in rstan given the row_vector restriction in the multi_normal function.
> > >
> > > 2. As my data has to be structured the way it is set up, I wonder whether there is a work around for me? I saw that the issue (#589) is fixed on the development platform.

> > > Please find attached my stan code; a matlab file that simulates data; the matlab data output (mat file); the code that runs the rstan model. Note that R.matlab has to be installed to read the mat file into R.

> > > For some reason the file upload isn't working, here's a dropbox link: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/hx7gqkcy3b3sjah/AACIyOcjzXmNY76Xx89d0mf4a

> > > Thank you very much for your help in advance!
> > >
> > > Daniel

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] external functions in user-defined Stan functions?
messages.body_plain:
Correct.  The user-defined functions are user-defined in Stan's
function definition syntax.

It is possible to integrate external functions written in C++, but
you need to be able to compute their gradients with respect to every
input that is going to be a parameter.  Usually R functions
don't come with gradients and are not templated in such a way
that we can use them with auto-diff.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.body_plain:
The problem here isn’t geometry (curvature, etc) but rather topology (shape of the manifold).
It’s easy to put together algorithms that will bounce around a hypersphere but it’s much harder
to implement an algorithm that follows the probability mass on the hypersphere.  There’s a reason
circular statistics is a notoriously difficult field!

For example, when constructing a trajectory on the hypersphere we have to be careful because
we can’t define a global coordinate system.  As Simon has shown you have to be careful when trying
to implement HMC on spaces that aren’t topologically equivalent to R^{n}, such as hyperspheres
and Grassmannian manifolds.  There are interesting approaches around, but none would fit
cleanly into our existing framework — for example how would we run HMC when some parameters
lie on a hypersphere while others lie in R^{n}?

And ensemble methods aren’t going to help.  You’re shooting a shotgun in the dark, and the number
of shot would have to increase exponentially with the dimension of the posterior.

On Jun 26, 2014, at 4:44 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> My geometric intuition is terrible, but I'm thinking
> it's the more general Riemann manifold case that's tricky.
>
> And the issue is whether it does the right thing with
> non-constant curvature.  For instance, will it enable the
> ensemble methods to sample from the funnel or the banana the way
> RHMC does?
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jun 26, 2014, at 5:23 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
>
>> Let me try to remember what I did for differential evolution on hypersphere. If you have point A, B and C on surface of hypershere, and want to move from A to A + (B-C):
>>
>>
>> - reflect A in B to get A'
>> - reflect A' in C to get A''
>> - reflect A'' in A to get A'''
>> - split A and A'''
>>
>> Simples!
>>
>> Easy enough also to do A + a(B-C)
>>
>>
>> On Thursday, 26 June 2014 12:49:46 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Oops --- this one got hung up in my drafts.
>>
>> I think the sphere is the first step to understanding
>> more general manifold cases.  So it'd be natural to do
>> spheres and then a more general Riemannian manifold case.
>>
>> Simon Byrne gave a nice talk at MCMski about HMC on a sphere
>> with geodesics (great circles in the spherical case).
>>
>> I don't think the spheres are too tricky for either Goodman
>> and Weare's walker moves or differential evolution updates.
>>
>> I'm sure Michael could knock out the general definitions
>> for these ensemble methods if he were so inclined.
>>
>> For the Goodman and Weare case, the volume adjustment for
>> Metropolis is going to be tricky (you move along a line there
>> and need to look at masses of neighborhoods on either end).
>>
>> For differential evolution, I think you're going to need something
>> like parallel transport (as seen in Michael's generalization of NUTS)
>> in order to apply a line of movement between two randomly selected points
>> to a third point.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>

>>
>>> This is probably completely useless comment, but I once had fun looking at a differential evolution algorithm on the surface of a hypersphere. It was to do with optimising the direction in a REML problem.

>>> it work with the addition of some clever priors.

>>>> Hi Mike,
>>>>
>>>> I think the answer you are looking for is in the Stan manual, section "Automatic Relevance Detection" (p.147 of the Stan 2.2.0 manual). It basically boils down to allowing rho to vary by dimension. In your case, the two values of rho pertaining to space would be the same, and the third value of rho pertaining to time would be allowed to be estimated separately. Your suggestion of using two additive GPs would mean you would also allow eta to vary between time and space. I'm not sure whether this is necessary; it would add an extra parameter to the model that you might not need.
>>>>

>>>>
>>>> Luc

Hey Guys,

I've successfully got my model to work! Very exciting.. Now I'd like to forecast my time series. I can't find any documentation to do this (no results come up when searching for "forecasting" in stan reference). Can someone suggest a place to look?

Thanks,
Sam

Also, code that worked is pasted below. It takes about 2 hours to complete...if anyone knows how to speed that up please let me know.

ode1=
  "data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=1> K;
vector[K] y[N];

  int<lower=1>  S;
  int<lower=1>  dum[N]; // monthly dummies

}
parameters {
corr_matrix[K] OmegaV;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauV;
corr_matrix[K] OmegaW;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauW;
vector[K] theta[N];

vector[K]  alpha[S];
vector[K] mu[N];
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_mu;

}
transformed parameters{
matrix[K,K] L_betaV;
matrix[K,K] L_betaW;

L_betaV <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaV);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaV[k1,k2] <- tauV[k1] * L_betaV[k1,k2];

L_betaW <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaW);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaW[k1,k2] <- tauW[k1] * L_betaW[k1,k2];

}

model{
//prior
mu[1] ~ normal(0, 1.0e+5 );
theta[1]~normal(y[1], 100);
y[1]~multi_normal_cholesky(theta[1], L_betaV);

//likelihood
for(n in 2:N){

mu[n]~normal(mu[n-1], sigma_mu);
theta[n]~multi_normal_cholesky(mu[n]+theta[n-1],L_betaW);
y[n]~multi_normal_cholesky(alpha[ dum[n] ]  + theta[n],L_betaV);

}

}

"

messages.body_plain:
We talk about forecasting as "predictive inference".  We should
add the "forecasting" terminology to aid in search.  We talk about it in the
description of Bayesian inference in the intro and later on, and in a bunch of
examples, such as Gaussian processes and naive Bayes.  I added a note
to the next manual issue to add an example for regression and time series:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/668#issuecomment-47424210

There are two ways to do this.

Both involve adding new data variables for the number of items to
predict/forecast and any inputs necessary to do that prediction.
Then you can either:

1.  Define new parameters for the predictions and give these parameters
predictions just like in the original model.  This only works for continous
predictions.

2.  Define new generated quantity variables for the predictions and
define them using random number generators in the generated quantities block.
This will work for discrete or continous predictions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
messages.body_plain:
OK, I see what's going on.  This is NOT a good way to code
these models.  This model relies on Andrew's trick for BUGS of
specifying an ill-defined posterior to sample from, then
attempting to pull it all back into something with reasonable
n_eff and Rhat through standardization.  Here's the offending
code in our example:

> transformed parameters {
>  vector[J] a;
>  vector[K] b;
>  vector[K] g;
>  vector[N] p;
>  real scale;
>  real shift;
>
>  shift <- mean(a);
>  scale <- sd(a);

>  a <- (a_raw - shift) / scale;
>  b <- (b_raw - shift) / scale;
>  g <- g_raw * scale;
>
>  for (n in 1:N)
>    p[n]<-g[kk[n]]*(a[jj[n]] - b[kk[n]]);

The problem here is that the raw values are not identified.

The problem is that the posterior for the parameters is improper.
And what you see is that Stan's HMC is effcient enough to race all over
the posterior and at least realize it's undefined.

There's a chapter on problematic posteriors that goes through
an example of the effects of such non-identified models.  (Look at the
plot of the long ridge, which is what happens for this kind of example.)

This model needs to be recoded so that it's properly identified.

We're working on rewriting all the ARM models, which are a pretty direct translation
of what's in Gelman and Hill, and thus not guaranteed to work.

This looks like a good place to start!

For models that don't have data we can release, we can simulate
data according to the model.  I want to bring up the question of how
to simulate predictors for regressions --- it seems like for proper testing
we shouldn't make them all independent.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
messages.body_plain:
The problem isn't the software but rather than the posterior
is improper in the parameters over which it's defined.

It doesn't really work with BUGS, either, when you look
at convergence of the raw parameters.  They'll drift like
they do in Stan.

In both BUGS and Stan, the transformed parameters may look
OK, but they're still problematically defined as transforms
of variables with improper posteriors.

The manual chapter on problematic posteriors goes over the
simplest possible example of where this can happen.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It's a reparameterization.  You have an
additive non-identifiability, which you can fix
by fixing one of the coefficients.  And you have
a multiplicative non-identifiability that can get
fixed by fixing one of the scales, say the student
abilities, to normal(0,1).  And then there's a sign
non-identifiability, which you can fix by constraining
the discrimination (g) to b positive.  (Unless it's
an item-response model, then I'm not sure what to do
about the sign --- Andrew and Jennifer discuss in their
book.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
messages.body_plain:
For ideal point models, Gelman and Hill discuss an approach to deal with reflection invariance using group level regression predictors. Simon Jackman has an example ("legislators") on his website that implements the approach in Winbugs. http://jackman.stanford.edu/mcmc/index.php. I would be very interested to see how to code a similar model in STAN but for a two-dimensional case. In two dimensions, two more indeterminacy arise if I am not mistaken: label switching and rotational indeterminacy.

On Saturday, June 28, 2014 1:02:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It's a reparameterization.  You have an
> additive non-identifiability, which you can fix
> by fixing one of the coefficients.  And you have
> a multiplicative non-identifiability that can get
> fixed by fixing one of the scales, say the student
> abilities, to normal(0,1).  And then there's a sign
> non-identifiability, which you can fix by constraining
> the discrimination (g) to b positive.  (Unless it's
> an item-response model, then I'm not sure what to do
> about the sign --- Andrew and Jennifer discuss in their
> book.)
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jun 28, 2014, at 5:25 PM, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > I'm confused how you would fix this. If you look at how it all gets computed in p[i] for example, g(a-b) leaves you with just (a_raw - b_raw)*g_raw so why even bother shifting and scaling? And what's the point of d? Or is this all some kind of reparameterization trick?
> >
> >
> > On Sat, Jun 28, 2014 at 7:50 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > OK, I see what's going on.  This is NOT a good way to code
> > these models.  This model relies on Andrew's trick for BUGS of
> > specifying an ill-defined posterior to sample from, then
> > attempting to pull it all back into something with reasonable
> > n_eff and Rhat through standardization.  Here's the offending
> > code in our example:
> >
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >  vector[J] a;
> > >  vector[K] b;
> > >  vector[K] g;
> > >  vector[N] p;
> > >  real scale;
> > >  real shift;
> > >
> > >  shift <- mean(a);
> > >  scale <- sd(a);
> >
> > >  a <- (a_raw - shift) / scale;
> > >  b <- (b_raw - shift) / scale;
> > >  g <- g_raw * scale;
> > >
> > >  for (n in 1:N)
> > >    p[n]<-g[kk[n]]*(a[jj[n]] - b[kk[n]]);
> >
> >
> > The problem here is that the raw values are not identified.
> >
> > The problem is that the posterior for the parameters is improper.
> > And what you see is that Stan's HMC is effcient enough to race all over
> > the posterior and at least realize it's undefined.
> >
> > There's a chapter on problematic posteriors that goes through
> > an example of the effects of such non-identified models.  (Look at the
> > plot of the long ridge, which is what happens for this kind of example.)
> >
> > This model needs to be recoded so that it's properly identified.
> >
> > We're working on rewriting all the ARM models, which are a pretty direct translation
> > of what's in Gelman and Hill, and thus not guaranteed to work.
> >
> > This looks like a good place to start!
> >
> > For models that don't have data we can release, we can simulate
> > data according to the model.  I want to bring up the question of how
> > to simulate predictors for regressions --- it seems like for proper testing
> > we shouldn't make them all independent.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > On Jun 27, 2014, at 12:28 AM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > So I manged to fit the model but  I always see to get a very low number of effective samples for the scaled variance and location parameters.Is that a reason to be concerned here? I have attached the model and here is a part of  the output.

> > > mu_gamma     0.8     0.3 0.5  0.3  0.5  0.7  1.2   1.9    3  2.5

messages.subject: Problem installing v2.3.0 on Mac OS X Mavericks
messages.subject_clean: Problem installing v2.3.0 on Mac OS X Mavericks
messages.body_plain:
You might recall that I had difficulty getting the last version of Stan to run on my MacBook. I was running into the same compilation error with v2.3.0, but I deleted -I/usr/local/include from CPPFLAGS in R's Makeconf file and the compile works fine. I also tested the schools example, and it worked too.

The problem arises because I have a version of Boost installed under /usr/local/include, the version I have is in some way incompatible with the version being used for RStan, and the compiler is finding the /usr/local/include version before it finds the one distributed with RStan.

I'm not sure how to fix that incompatibility for others who might encounter it, but it might be worth mentioning this in the documentation somewhere if there isn't a simple way around it.

Kent

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.body_plain:
But maybe DREAM-type MCMC algorithms work on the surface of a hypershere, if you do what I suggest above and do differences by reflection?

ps. recent work I have done using DREAM integrated with NUTS is interesting - but makes sense. One of my conclusions is that some of the hoops you have to go through with DREAM are not needed if integrated with NUTS. Also I could implement a dual averaging for the difference operator size, and can adjust the proportion of NUTS and DREAM according to the curvature of the space.

Maybe I'll describe this to Michael when we meet in London soon.

On Friday, 27 June 2014 10:10:26 UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The problem here isn’t geometry (curvature, etc) but rather topology (shape of the manifold).
> It’s easy to put together algorithms that will bounce around a hypersphere but it’s much harder
> to implement an algorithm that follows the probability mass on the hypersphere.  There’s a reason
> circular statistics is a notoriously difficult field!
>
> For example, when constructing a trajectory on the hypersphere we have to be careful because
> we can’t define a global coordinate system.  As Simon has shown you have to be careful when trying
> to implement HMC on spaces that aren’t topologically equivalent to R^{n}, such as hyperspheres
> and Grassmannian manifolds.  There are interesting approaches around, but none would fit
> cleanly into our existing framework — for example how would we run HMC when some parameters
> lie on a hypersphere while others lie in R^{n}?
>
> And ensemble methods aren’t going to help.  You’re shooting a shotgun in the dark, and the number
> of shot would have to increase exponentially with the dimension of the posterior.
>
> On Jun 26, 2014, at 4:44 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > My geometric intuition is terrible, but I'm thinking
> > it's the more general Riemann manifold case that's tricky.
> >
> > And the issue is whether it does the right thing with
> > non-constant curvature.  For instance, will it enable the
> > ensemble methods to sample from the funnel or the banana the way
> > RHMC does?
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Jun 26, 2014, at 5:23 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Let me try to remember what I did for differential evolution on hypersphere. If you have point A, B and C on surface of hypershere, and want to move from A to A + (B-C):
> >>
> >>
> >> - reflect A in B to get A'
> >> - reflect A' in C to get A''
> >> - reflect A'' in A to get A'''
> >> - split A and A'''
> >>
> >> Simples!
> >>
> >> Easy enough also to do A + a(B-C)
> >>
> >>
> >> On Thursday, 26 June 2014 12:49:46 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> Oops --- this one got hung up in my drafts.
> >>
> >> I think the sphere is the first step to understanding
> >> more general manifold cases.  So it'd be natural to do
> >> spheres and then a more general Riemannian manifold case.
> >>
> >> Simon Byrne gave a nice talk at MCMski about HMC on a sphere
> >> with geodesics (great circles in the spherical case).
> >>
> >> I don't think the spheres are too tricky for either Goodman
> >> and Weare's walker moves or differential evolution updates.
> >>
> >> I'm sure Michael could knock out the general definitions
> >> for these ensemble methods if he were so inclined.
> >>
> >> For the Goodman and Weare case, the volume adjustment for
> >> Metropolis is going to be tricky (you move along a line there
> >> and need to look at masses of neighborhoods on either end).
> >>
> >> For differential evolution, I think you're going to need something
> >> like parallel transport (as seen in Michael's generalization of NUTS)
> >> in order to apply a line of movement between two randomly selected points
> >> to a third point.
> >>
> >> - Bob
> >>
> >>
> >> On Jun 20, 2014, at 12:25 AM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
> >>
> >>> This is probably completely useless comment, but I once had fun looking at a differential evolution algorithm on the surface of a hypersphere. It was to do with optimising the direction in a REML problem.
> >>>
> >>> The idea was to convert the difference into some reflections.
> >>>
> >>> It didn't seem to help the method much -{
> >>>
> >>>
> >>> On Thursday, 19 June 2014 21:41:13 UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >>> As Luc notes the first step would be letting each variable have its own rho.
> >>>
> >>> Spherical coordinates are going to be tricky because they have a different topology
> >>> than what Stan can naively handle (S^{n - 1} vs R^{n}).  I'm not sure there's a great
> >>> answer yet -- although there had previously been some thoughts on how to make
> >>> it work with the addition of some clever priors.
> >>>
> >>> On Jun 19, 2014, at 6:28 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>>> Hi Mike,
> >>>>
> >>>> I think the answer you are looking for is in the Stan manual, section "Automatic Relevance Detection" (p.147 of the Stan 2.2.0 manual). It basically boils down to allowing rho to vary by dimension. In your case, the two values of rho pertaining to space would be the same, and the third value of rho pertaining to time would be allowed to be estimated separately. Your suggestion of using two additive GPs would mean you would also allow eta to vary between time and space. I'm not sure whether this is necessary; it would add an extra parameter to the model that you might not need.
> >>>>
> >>>> Best,
> >>>>
> >>>> Luc
> >>>>
> >>>> On Thursday, 19 June 2014 08:26:29 UTC-7, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> >>>> Hi folks,
> >>>>
> >>>> I'm finally getting to grips with GPs, and am now looking at the
> >>>> multivariate case for application to my real-world data. Specifically,
> >>>> I deal with EEG data where we get measure voltage as a function of
> >>>> time and position on the skull. Taking a simple spherical model of the
> >>>> skull, we can encode position in terms of longitude and latitude (or
> >>>> phi & theta if you want to use polar coordinates). I see from the
> >>>> example in the manual how to combine two variables where simple
> >>>> euclidean distance is computed, i.e. (pg 144):
> >>>>
> >>>>     data {
> >>>>       int<lower=1> D;
> >>>>       int<lower=1> N;
> >>>>       vector[D] x[N];
> >>>>     }
> >>>>     transformed data {
> >>>>     ...
> >>>>           Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-dot_self(x[i] - x[j]))
> >>>>                         + if_else(i==j, 0.1, 0.0);
> >>>>     ...
> >>>>
> >>>> Any ideas on how to do this with one simple continuous variate (time)
> >>>> and spherical coordinates?
> >>>>
> >>>> Also, if I move to a fitting/inference context where I evaluate the GP
> >>>> hyperparamters (eta, sigma, rho), presumably something should be done
> >>>> to reflect the fact that time and spatial coordinates are very
> >>>> different metrics and therefore might have different best-suited
> >>>> hyperparameter values, no? The obvious solution would be to have two
> >>>> additive GPs, one for time and one for the spherical coordinate, and
> >>>> thus two sets of GP hyperparameters, but I don't want to assume that
> >>>> the same temporal function exists at all spatial coordinates and vice
> >>>> versa. Any thoughts?
> >>>>
> >>>> Thanks in advance,
> >>>>
> >>>> Mike

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
messages.body_plain:
On Jun 30, 2014, at 1:12 AM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:

> But maybe DREAM-type MCMC algorithms work on the surface of a hypershere, if you do what I suggest above and do differences by reflection?

Yes, you can do that.  Then your moves will be legal and geometrically
sensible if you have a uniform distribution on the surface of a sphere.

But what happens when you have another term in the density?  Then you
need to move to a geometry based on the curvature of the log probability.
I think that's what Michael means by saying it's easy to move on the sphere,
but hard to follow the probability mass.

So I think you'd need to generalize the algorithm along the lines of
RHMC to general metrics.  I'm not good enough at geometry to do that.
Maybe I should make it a stretch goal (sorry, that pun was intentional).

- Bob

Thanks Arnold,

I tried to implement your code but for some reason I keep getting an error message "Error in function stan::prob::bernoulli_logit_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Logit transformed probability parameter[0]  is 1.#QNAN:0, but must not be nan!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density."

I have tried many things but nothing seems to work. I have attached the code. The indices in the data block are the following

p2 <- 7
p2_idx <- 1:7
c2 <- 8
c2_idx <- 8:15
p3 <- 8
p3_idx <- 8:15
c3 <- 7
c3_idx <- 1:7

Rick,

On Saturday, June 28, 2014 4:11:40 PM UTC-4, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> You're going to have to do something similar. There's no NA in stan or indexing, so you have to come up with ways to make the indexing easy. There are several ways of doing what you want to do. One way of doing what you want is have beta2 and beta3 be transformed parameters of length 7. For beta2 you'd set of the group you'd want to drop to 0.  Here's an example that only uses beta2.
>
>
>
> data {
>   int n_groups; // number of groups (in the example 7)
>
>   int beta2_const_n; // number of entries in beta2 set to 0
>
>   int beta2_const_idx[beta2_obs_n]; // indices of entries in beta2 to set to 0
>
>   int beta2_param_n; // number of entries in beta2 that are parameters
>
>   int beta2_param_idx[beta2_obs_n]; // indices of entries in beta2 that are parameters
>
>   ...
>
> }
> parameters {
>
>   vector[n_groups] beta1;
>
>   vector[beta2_param_n] beta2_param;
>
>   ...
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   vector[N] p;
>
>   vector[n_groups] beta2;
>
>
>
>   for (i in 1:beta2_const_n) {
>
>     beta2[beta2_const_idx[i]] <- 0.0;
>
>   }
>   for (i in 1:beta2_param_n) {
>
>     beta2[beta2_param_idx[i]] <- beta2_param[i];
>
>   }
>
>
>   for (i in 1:N) {
>
>     p[i] <- beta1[kk[n]] * x1[gg[n]]] + beta2[kk[n]] * x2[gg[n]];
>
>   }
>
>   ...
> }
>
> ...
>
>
> and the data you'd pass to it would be generated in R as,
>
>
> n_groups <- 7
> beta2_const_n <- 4
> beta2_const_idx <- c(3, 6, 7)
> beta2_param_n <- 3
> beta2_param_idx <- c(1, 2, 4)
>
> The above is equivalent to doing the following manually,
>
>
> beta2[1] <- beta2_param[1];
>
> beta2[2] <- beta2_param[2];
> beta2[3] <- 0.0;
>
> beta2[4] <- beta2_param[3];
> beta2[5] <- 0.0;
>
> beta2[6] <- 0.0;
> beta2[7] <- 0.0;
>
>
> but I presented it in a more general form that would scale to larger numbers of groups and allowing the model to be reused with different numbers of groups.  In general, I try to preprocess the data as much as possible outside of Stan, so that the model does as little data manipulation as is necessary.
>
>
> Similar ideas are discussed in the section on Missing Data in the Stan manual.  When you are dropping the coefficient for some groups, it is equivalent to constraining it to 0.
>
>
